items.title: Inteligência artificial e o impacto nas relações de trabalho
items.abstract: This study aims to analyze the extent to which current Brazilian labor legislation is sufficient to protect workers subject to algorithmic management through artificial intelligence systems. It seeks to understand the impact of these technologies on labor relations, particularly regarding legal subordination, control mechanisms, and the risks arising from their use. To this end, qualitative bibliographic and documentary research was conducted through the analysis of legislation, legal scholarship, scientific articles, institutional documents, and case law related to artificial intelligence and worker protection. The results demonstrate that Brazilian legislation provides legal instruments capable of protecting workers against algorithmic management, particularly Articles 2, 3, and 6, sole paragraph, of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), as well as provisions concerning non-pecuniary damages and civil liability. The study also found that algorithmic subordination may constitute legal subordination, since computerized systems can perform command, control, and supervision functions. However, challenges were identified regarding the effectiveness of legal protection, judicial interpretation, and liability for damages arising from these technologies. It is concluded that the Brazilian legal system provides an adaptable normative framework for worker protection, but its effectiveness depends on the proper application of existing legal provisions, the development of case law, and the ability to address the challenges posed by technological advancement.

items.title: Inteligencia artificial y personalización del aprendizaje en la educación básica: oportunidades y desafíos. una revisión de alcance
items.abstract: Introduction. Artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for personalized learning in basic education through tools capable of adapting content, providing feedback, and addressing diverse educational needs. The objective of this study was to analyze artificial intelligence applications in personalized learning, identifying pedagogical opportunities, implementation challenges, and research trends. Methodology. A scoping review was developed following the methodological guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute and the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The bibliographic selection exercise covered publications from 2020 to 2026, considering Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and SciELO. Results. The methodological flow included 420 identified records, 90 duplicates removed, and 330 records screened. Following the screening and eligibility stages, a set of 25 studies was established for thematic synthesis. The results were organized into five categories: adaptive systems and intelligent tutoring, generative artificial intelligence, AI literacy and teacher mediation, equity and ethics, and implementation and evaluation. The literature examined revealed opportunities related to content adaptation, individualized support, immediate feedback, and academic progress monitoring. Challenges associated with data protection, algorithmic bias, digital inequalities, and teacher preparation were also identified. Conclusions. It is concluded that artificial intelligence offers relevant possibilities for diversifying learning experiences, although its educational integration requires pedagogical supervision, ethical criteria, and contextualized evaluations to establish its actual contributions.

items.title: Intelligent Disease Outbreak Risk Assessment Using Generative AI and Collaborative Multi-Agent Systems
items.abstract: Disease-outbreak information is spread across surveillance reports, environmental observations and population statistics,and public-health users need it presented in a form they can inspectand question. This paper presents the design and implementationof an SDG 3 health platform that combines a multi-factor outbreak risk-scoring module, a what-if climate-variation analysis, acollaborative multi-agent chatbot, a locally hosted Mistral 7B Instruct model accessed through LM Studio, a retrieval-groundedknowledge module, and a heuristic hallucination detector for usersubmitted outbreak reports. The risk module combines new cases,rainfall, humidity, temperature, population density and hospitaladmissions into a weighted score from 0 to 100, classifies it as Low,Medium or High, and derives four-week and three-month projections. A React front end communicates with a FastAPI back endthat provides JWT authentication, role-based access, an administrator review workflow with audit events, and report generation. Thelanguage model communicates information only; it does not compute risk scores. The platform does not forecast case counts witha time-series model. A Random Forest classifier for risk-categoryclassification (Low, Medium, High) was evaluated on a balancedtest set of 90 samples and reached 88.89% accuracy and a macroF1-score of 88.89%. The worked examples of the scoring rules arenot accuracy measurements, and learned time-series forecasting,such as LSTM, is identified as future work.Keywords—Disease outbreak risk assessment, generative AI, multiagent systems, Mistral, LM Studio, retrieval-augmented generation,hallucination detection, public health, SDG 3.

items.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
items.abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.

items.title: Interpersonal academic help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency: the roles of stigma, shame, and perceived anonymity
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has emerged as a new source of academic support for university students. However, students' willingness to seek academic help may also be influenced by social evaluation concerns surrounding traditional interpersonal help-seeking. This study examines how academic help-seeking (AHS) stigma relates to interpersonal help-seeking avoidance through academic shame, and whether interpersonal avoidance is associated with GAI help-seeking tendency under different levels of perceived anonymity. Methods Two independent cross-sectional survey studies were conducted among Chinese university students. Study 1 examined the relationships among AHS stigma, academic shame, and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance using data from 183 undergraduate students. Study 2 extended the model with a sample of 401 university students by examining the relationship between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency, as well as the moderating role of perceived anonymity. PLS-SEM was used to test the proposed relationships. Results Across both studies, AHS stigma was positively associated with interpersonal help-seeking avoidance. Academic shame showed significant indirect associations between AHS stigma and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance in both studies. Study 2 further showed that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance was positively associated with GAI help-seeking tendency. Moreover, perceived anonymity positively moderated this relationship, such that the positive association between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency was stronger at higher levels of perceived anonymity. Discussion The findings highlight the social-emotional dimensions of academic help-seeking, showing that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance can coexist with a greater willingness to seek support from GAI tools. Perceived anonymity further conditions this association, suggesting that the perceived social visibility of help-seeking is relevant to students' support preferences. These findings extend the understanding of GAI-assisted academic help-seeking beyond technology-related considerations, while distinguishing help-seeking tendencies from actual changes in support-source use.

items.title: Interpretive model of emotional expression in sculptural works based on visual-affective semantic analysis
items.abstract: The expression of emotions in sculptures is conveyed through structural forms, spatial relationships, material characteristics, and symbolic elements. However, traditional artistic analysis mainly relies on expert interpretation, making emotional expression difficult to quantify. With the development of computer vision and multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI), deep learning approaches provide new opportunities for visual art understanding. Nevertheless, existing methods still face challenges in establishing connections between visual features and abstract emotional semantics, as well as providing interpretable prediction processes. To address these issues, an interpretive model of emotional expression in sculptures based on visual-affective semantic analysis is proposed. A public sculpture image dataset containing 1,800 instances is constructed. A 50-layer Residual Network (ResNet50) is employed to extract morphological and textural features, while Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) is used to establish associations between visual representations and affective semantics. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates visual and semantic features for emotion classification. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and semantic ablation methods are further applied to analyze the decision-making process of the model. Experimental results show that the visual-semantic fusion model achieves an accuracy of 82.59% and a Macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 80.73% on the test set, outperforming the ResNet50 visual model with 76.30% accuracy and 75.67% Macro-F1, as well as the CLIP semantic model with 73.85% accuracy and 72.58% Macro-F1. Interpretation analysis demonstrates that the model mainly focuses on essential artistic elements, including posture, contour, and spatial structure, with strong consistency with expert evaluations. This research provides an effective artificial intelligence framework for sculptural emotion analysis and offers potential applications in digital museums, art education, intelligent retrieval systems, and computational cultural heritage studies.

items.title: Irreducible-Realization Classification Protecting a Settled Model: How Calling a Result Improbable Can Keep a Model From Reopening
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Irreducible-Realization Classification Protecting a Settled Model, a mechanism through which calling a surprising result ordinary variation can keep a model or one of its assumptions from being reopened. The mechanism applies when the classification itself prevents diagnostic inquiry and the model’s account of uncertainty gives inadequate grounds for that decision. The paper asks what the model projected, what range or probability distribution supported that projection, and how the observed departure compared with it. A well-supported account of uncertainty can justify leaving a model in place after a surprising result. Possibility alone gives little guidance about whether a departure of this size warrants investigation. Identifying the mechanism also requires evidence that the classification actually stopped inquiry. A public description of a result as bad luck can coexist with an investigation already underway. The paper places the mechanism alongside Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s account of highly improbable events and examines two documented cases. Casino consultant Eliot Jacobson recalled initially attributing a report about the Lucky Lucky blackjack side bet to ordinary variation. Further reports prompted an analysis showing that players could gain an advantage by choosing when to bet. The published accounts provide no casino results from which to estimate the probability of the initial report. The 2011 OPERA neutrino measurement illustrates a different response. The apparent early arrival was large relative to the stated timing uncertainties, and the collaboration invited scrutiny. Subsequent investigation traced the anomaly to a fault in the fiber-optic timing system. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can inspect the uncertainty estimate behind a decision to close an inquiry. A potential application in human–AI evaluation is a transit planner’s review of an unexpectedly long wait. If the planner closes the review because an AI forecast allows occasional delays, an evaluator could ask how often the forecast predicted waits that long under comparable conditions and what evidence supported that estimate.

items.title: Islamic Financial Planning for Inclusive and Sustainable Wellbeing
items.abstract: Backgrounds: Islamic financial planning can connect household resilience, ethical investment and social redistribution within a coherent life-cycle framework. Objectives: This article updates the supplied manuscript by integrating comparative documentary evidence from Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Indonesia, Türkiye and Pakistan with a proposed digitally enabled operational model. Methodology: A structured narrative review distinguishes observed institutional developments from normative design choices and untested impact propositions. Findings: The model retains four interdependent pillars: wealth protection, accumulation, preservation and distribution. It adds explicit cash flow management, affordable access, consumer protection and measurable wellbeing outcomes. Contemporary official evidence demonstrates the scale of Islamic finance and the feasibility of retail sukuk, social takaful, value-based intermediation and cash waqf-linked sukuk, but does not establish that a comprehensive planning service has caused improvements in household welfare. Blockchain, artificial intelligence, machine learning, the Internet of Things and big data can support traceability, forecasting and monitoring when governed by consent, legal enforceability, Shariah review and human accountability. The article proposes a mind map, implementation sequence and evaluation design. Conclusions: Universal access is a central service principle; religion-specific obligations and legally restricted funds require separate treatment. The resulting framework offers testable pathways toward financial resilience and sustainable development without assuming guaranteed returns or uniform effects.

items.title: Jailbreak Detection on Large Language Models via Contrastive Prototype Structures
items.abstract: Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

items.title: Kisan Sahayak: A Smart Agricultural Marketplace for Connecting Farmers, Labourers, and Machinery Providers
items.abstract: Agricultural activities depend on the timely coordi-nation of land, labour, machinery, information, and local services. In many rural settings, farmers identify workers and equipment through personal contacts and fragmented communication chan-nels. Such methods can make it difficult to discover available service providers beyond an immediate network, communicate work requirements consistently, and maintain a clear record of requests. Agricultural labourers and machinery owners can face a corresponding difficulty in communicating their availability to potential customers. This paper presents Kisan Sahayak, a theoretical, mobile-first agricultural marketplace designed to connect farmers, labourers, and machinery providers through a common web platform. The proposed system is organized around the MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js (MERN) stack. Its conceptual capabilities include role-based profiles, location-aware discovery, farmer job postings, direct worker invitations, request acceptance or rejec-tion, wage negotiation, machinery listings, and service-request tracking. An optional artificial-intelligence assistance layer is proposed for multilingual platform guidance and explainable matching based on location, skills, availability, and stated pref-erences. The paper details the system architecture, data model, stake-holder workflows, marketplace rules, AI design, security and privacy controls, deployment considerations, and an evaluation framework. The contribution is an architectural and process model; no field trial, measured performance result, or im-plemented AI capability is claimed. The design is intended to provide a foundation for subsequent implementation and empirical evaluation in agricultural communities

items.title: Knowing What You Know: A Trait Theory of Reviewer Value in Human-AI Cognitive Systems
items.abstract: When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

items.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
items.abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

items.title: Künstliche Intelligenz in der Produktionstechnik: Potenziale, Anwendungen und gesellschaftliche Perspektiven
items.abstract: This chapter conceptualizes artificial intelligence (AI) in production engineering as a sociotechnical innovation. AI not only promises efficiency gains but also fundamentally reorganizes knowledge, work, and responsibility. Three case studies from assembly planning, laser beam welding, and predictive maintenance illustrate how algorithmic systems interact with embodied experiential knowledge and which value-laden decisions are embedded in objectives, thresholds, and routines. The analysis links technical core intuitions with perspectives on tacit knowledge, rationalization, and situated practice. A synthesis reveals three key tensions: the transformation of experience into formalized model knowledge, the shift of responsibility towards system design and operation, and the change in competency profiles towards data literacy and judgment competence. Regulatory requirements and organizational governance provide the guardrails for legitimacy and safety. From this, design principles are derived for trustworthy, auditable, and empowering AI that consistently combines transparency, human oversight, qualification, and organizational embedding.

items.title: La formación del profesorado universitario ante la inteligencia artificial: una articulación teórica entre autonomía, mediación pedagógica y calidad educativa
items.abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education compels us to look beyond faculty members’ technological skills: it demands that we rethink the criteria that guide their professional judgment. With this in mind, this article builds a theoretical bridge between continuing education, pedagogical mediation, intellectual autonomy, and quality management, using Venezuelan universities as a case study. Through a critical review of academic literature, regulations, and international frameworks, the study identifies four interdependent pillars: professional identity linked to lifelong learning; pedagogical mediation under strict human supervision; ethical responsibility toward the sociocultural environment; and the institutional conditions necessary to sustain this innovation. Building on this, the study proposes integrating the dimensions of Being, Doing, Owing to Be, and Wanting to Be as a reflective compass for educators. In essence, it argues that educational quality does not improve through mere automation; rather, it requires pedagogical decisions to guide it, an awareness of its limits, and equitable access. Therefore, training teachers in AI requires a deeply humanistic and critical approach, supported by institutional policies that ensure responsible development and evaluation.

items.title: Large Language Models or AI Agents for English to Arabic Translation? An assessment on WikiEn-Ar190
items.abstract: This research investigates whether a large language model or an autonomous AI Agent performs better at translating from English to Arabic, which is considered a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new dataset of 190 carefully selected Wikipedia articles from 18 different areas, which were created and verified by two native Arabic speakers to ensure that they accurately reflect both meaning and style. Using this dataset, the study evaluates the translation quality of GPT-5-mini both as an independent neural translator and when used within a more complex process that includes self-assessment and improvement. As a standalone model, GPT-5-mini produced very fluent translations , achieving a COMET score of 0.8649 and receiving high human scores for adequacy, fluency, and style (averaging 4.53 out of 5). When used in a system that combined translation with self-assessment, it improved lexical accuracy by 28.76% (BLEU score of 22.83) while maintaining a similar level of semantic quality. These findings show that methods involving autonomous reasoning can improve translation consistency for language pairs with limited resources. Beyond the results, the approach offers a framework for evaluating and improving translations, potentially using them as assisting tools to expand the representation of low resource languages, such as Arabic, on the web.

items.title: Latent profile analysis of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates: associations with positive acceptance and striving
items.abstract: Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

items.title: Law and Artificial Intelligence: The Concept of Liability and Legal Certainty under Indonesian Legal Frameworks
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across key societal sectors presents profound legal challenges, particularly regarding liability attribution and legal certainty. Operating autonomously with non-deterministic decision-making capabilities, AI deployment gives rise to risks such as copyright infringement, privacy breaches, and misinformation. Employing a normative juridical research method, this article examines whether AI can be held legally accountable under Indonesian law and evaluates the current statutory framework’s capacity to maintain legal certainty. The analysis demonstrates that Indonesian jurisprudence does not recognize AI as an independent legal subject, as it lacks moral agency and free choice. Consequently, legal responsibility remains anchored in traditional legal subjects—natural persons and corporate entities—operating in the capacity of Electronic Agents or Electronic System Providers (ESPs). Legal liability for AI-induced harm is channeled back to human developers and operating entities through established doctrines of vicarious and strict liability. Furthermore, while Indonesia currently lacks a standalone AI statute, legal certainty is preserved through an interlocking, multi-layered regulatory regime, including the Copyright Law, the Personal Data Protection Law, the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, the new Penal Code, the Government Regulation on Operation of Electronic Systems and Transactions, and the Circular Letter of the Minister of Communication and Information Technology on Artificial Intelligence Ethics. This study concludes that existing statutory frameworks provide enforceable sanctions, emphasizing that legal subjects must maintain strict compliance to mitigate technology-induced harm.

items.title: Layout-Dependent Geometry of Relational Maps: How the Same Connections Can Take Different Shapes
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Layout-Dependent Geometry of Relational Maps, a structural constraint on what a viewer can infer from a diagram of connections. Two drawings can preserve the same station order and interchanges while giving the routes different lengths, placing stations at different distances, or making different groups stand out. A diagram may therefore give a passenger reliable grounds for choosing where to change trains while giving little indication of how far apart those stations lie above ground. The paper assesses a claim drawn from a map by asking whether the coding and layout preserve the particular relation the claim concerns. Redrawing a fixed set of connections can reveal which features change with placement. Even a cluster that persists across several drawings requires an independent check of what the positions encode. A claim about how viewers interpreted the cluster requires evidence about the viewers as well. The paper places this constraint alongside Jacques Bertin’s account of visual variables in graphics and examines two transit diagrams. Harry Beck’s 1933 London Underground diagram preserved station order and interchanges while redrawing distances. In a later study using London trip data from 1998 to 2005, Zhan Guo found that passengers were more likely to choose routes that appeared shorter on the map. The 1972 New York subway diagram, produced by Massimo Vignelli’s team at Unimark with Joan Charysyn as lead designer, drew Central Park as a square. The paper examines one rider’s complaint about wayfinding, John Tauranac’s criticism of the diagram’s geography, and its replacement in 1979. Part of the Equivalence and Interchangeability series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a prospective application in human–AI interaction. An AI assistant might draw a citation network from a set of papers. Readers can check a line between two papers against their references. If the assistant also claims that papers placed close together make similar arguments, that claim requires evidence from their texts or a placement rule that explicitly encodes such similarity.

items.title: Learning from an innovative, live, international simulation exercise comprising a medical evacuation system for high-consequence infectious diseases: SIMEX Volare
items.abstract: Background High consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) have high mortality rates and limited treatment options and require urgent co-ordinated public health response including sophisticated high-level isolation unit care. In the absence of a high-level isolation capacity in Ireland, the health systems of Ireland, Norway and Germany have agreed a collaborative HCID care arrangement where a patient diagnosed with a HCID in Ireland can be medically evacuated by Norwegian specialised air ambulance to Germany for ongoing care. These cross-border emergency arrangements and their coordination through EU mechanisms have not yet had to be exercised in real world circumstances. A full-scale real-time simulation exercise was devised to test pathways and use findings to improve the system. Methods This three-day, live, multi-service and cross-agency simulation tested multi-country interoperability, with over two hundred stakeholder participants. It was overseen by an international strategic exercise planning group and informed by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) simulation exercise cycle and national and ECDC guidance. Exercise evaluators assessed medical evacuation performance against predefined key performance indicators across the domains of international stakeholder activation, coordination and communication. Key Finding Such a large-scale exercise is resource-intensive, but feasible with cross-jurisdictional engagement. Intense cross-border planning was key to build relationships, clarify governance and develop harmonised guidance, pathways and procedures for testing in a safe environment. All eight high level objectives were achieved or partially achieved when measured against the pre-determined performance indicators. Findings including noting of discrepancies between different services in their high-level personal protective equipment (PPE) provision, and lack of 24-hour provision of services including laboratory diagnostics, specialised waste management, and occupational health. Lack of an agreed end-to-end transport protocol and waste-water management protocol required remedying. Following the exercise, strengthened governance and operational arrangements for preparedness and response include the development of a managed clinical network approach, enhanced operational capacity for key national services, and plans for a coordinated national HCID training and simulation programme. The findings have yielded key insights regarding interoperability across organisations and countries, and subsequent recommendations are likely to be transferable to other simulation programmes. To maintain optimal preparedness for high-stakes diseases and promote health security across Europe, partners should further incorporate international live simulation exercises to defend against cross-border health threats.

items.title: Learning how to use a Decision Support System: a simulation of Human-AI interaction frames.
items.abstract: The integration of AI in Decision Support System faces a hard limit: automation bias (Cummings, 2004). While AI may outperforms human operators in certain tasks, the added value of keeping humans-in-the-loop becomes questionable if they merely validate AI decisions. However, the ideal tool should enable complementary team performance (CTP). CTP describes a situation where the human-AI (HAI) team overcomes both AI capacity and the operator alone in terms of performance, which is incompatible with automation bias. CTP describes a one-time performance, and is not easy to achieve: it means operators stay on their mind mostly when they are correct, and change their mind mostly when the AI is correct, which is optimistic, as shown in a recent meta-analysis (Vaccaro et al., 2024).However, one observation of CTP doesn’t preclude automation bias in the long-run. Beyond a static conception of performance, the dynamics of these interactions have been studied through several theoretical perspectives (Kumar et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2023; Gonzalez et al., 2026).The stress is often put on the evolution of trust in AI through time (Chong et al., 2022), but the issue of learning effects in the task, independent of trust, is poorly understood. What is the impact of AI assistance on human skill acquisition? This question has been mostly answered in educational contexts (Fan et al., 2025; Kosmyna et al., 2025), where the delegation of cognitive tasks to the AI would hinder the learning process of the children. In operational contexts, the fear of deskilling is often expressed by experts like physicists (Natali et al., 2025), but empirical evidence is missing, to our knowledge. This gap in the literature is understandable as the inquiry is challenging: in any domain, future experts are few, their tasks to learn are numerous, and the deployment of measurement settings on long duration might be difficult.To explore this question without conducting such longitudinal studies, we propose to build a model of human learning of a technical task with an advisor. Our work develop a simulation setting on a classification task to depict possible quantitative effects of advice-taking on performance evolution through time. This modeling scheme allowed us to investigate the impact of the advisor on skill development. While most people expect that a more accurate advisor would lead the learner to higher performances, Vaccaro et al. (2024) suggest that advisors with lesser performance would be more prone to inducing CTP. This claim follows from static experimental contexts: we hereby test it in a dynamical setting. We expect that in the long-run, deskilling could happen, and would affect not-only degraded-mode performance, but also maximal running performance. Is the performance of the advisor the main factor determining performance evolution, or could the assistants have an intrinsic complementarity with the learner, depending on their classification patterns? The type of AI could lead to different results, in terms of performance, reliance, and of dependence.

items.title: Learning to Coordinate: LLM-Guided Workflow Evolution for Token-Efficient Red Teaming
items.abstract: Automated red teaming is essential for identifying safety failures in large language models (LLMs), but its practical scalability depends on the resources required to discover those failures. Multi-agent systems can combine complementary capabilities, yet repeated planning, redundant exchanges, and ineffective information routing can make their coordination expensive. Moreover, a target model's response indicates the outcome of a test without identifying which collaboration decision should change. We present Learning to Coordinate (L2C), an LLM-guided framework that evolves an executable multi-agent workflow for each red-teaming case. L2C represents agent responsibilities, execution dependencies, and input bindings in a versioned graph, and associates each graph with records of the information actually delivered and produced. A controller trained through supervised fine-tuning integrates these records with target responses, evaluator verdicts, and remaining budget to retain the workflow, refine instructions, restructure collaboration, or lock further editing. This design connects feedback to explicit changes in subsequent execution while allowing a useful organization to continue without repeated controller intervention. The evaluation protocol covers HarmBench with three execution backbones and two target models, together with component ablations, dataset transfer, and evaluator checks. Across the six executor-target configurations, L2C improves ASR over EvoSynth by 1.4 to 4.5 percentage points while reducing mean online tokens by 35.6% to 37.3%. L2C connects adaptive collaboration to the resource requirements of automated security evaluation.

items.title: Learning What to Degrade: A Recoverability-Aware Curriculum for Reliable Smart-Glasses Super-Resolution
items.abstract: Degradations in smart-glasses images obscure small text and fine-grained structures needed by vision-language models (VLMs) for visual assistance. We introduce an high-resolution (HR)-referenced semantic evaluation protocol that compares VLM outputs on restored images with those on corresponding HR references. Our evaluation reveals two failure modes: generative SR can synthesize misleading details, whereas restoration-oriented SR can leave critical evidence blurred or ambiguous. These findings motivate improving faithful detail recovery in restoration-oriented SR, where a key training challenge is to provide sufficiently difficult inputs while retaining recoverable visual information. We propose ReDiC (Recoverability-Difficulty Curriculum), which combines a model-independent recoverability proxy with model-relative restoration difficulty to adapt training degradation severity. ReDiC increases severity when inputs are recoverable and restoration is easy, maintains challenging but recoverable conditions, and reduces severity when estimated recoverability is low. It modifies only training degradation generation, leaving the SR architecture and reconstruction objective unchanged. Across NAFNet, SwinIR, and MambaIR, ReDiC improves average PSNR by approximately 2.5 dB and HR-referenced semantic scores by about 3 points over the corresponding baselines on synthetic benchmarks, with further gains confirmed by LLM-based and human evaluations on 200 real smart-glasses captures.

items.title: Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning
items.abstract: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.

items.title: Learning, leading, and innovating: Reimagining manual handling and musculoskeletal disorders as critical risks
items.abstract: Introduction Musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) account for 30% of workplace harm in Aotearoa New Zealand1. Traditional manual handling training often fails because it focuses on individual behaviour rather than system design2. In 2025, Foodstuffs South Island (FSSI) challenged the status quo by giving manual handling the same priority and attention as their critical risks, noting it represented 64% of their injury claims. Moving beyond a ‘tick-box’ compliance exercise, FSSI partnered with ProErgo+ to apply a systems-thinking, ergonomics approach to risk management. Methods A 10-member Manual Handling Task Force participated in four sessions jointly facilitated by FSSI and ProErgo+. We used a structured musculoskeletal risk management framework to identify, assess, and control risks. Data was gathered through discomfort and risk factor surveys, capturing both physical and psychosocial risks. To quantify physical demands, the New Zealand Manual Handling Assessment Charts (NZMAC)3 was used for the five highest-risk tasks. Findings and proposed controls were then presented to senior leadership. Results Of the 207 workers surveyed, 75% reported discomfort. The data revealed distinct psychosocial risks between Ambient and Temperature Controlled distribution centres. The NZMAC assessments successfully pinpointed specific high-risk task elements, allowing for targeted risk reduction rather than broad, ineffective interventions. Conclusion Managing work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WRMSDs) requires understanding the complex interactions of physical, psychosocial, environmental, organisational, and individual factors. This project succeeded by combining forward-thinking leadership with a collaborative co-design approach. By empowering workers as ‘experts’ and applying ergonomics principles, FSSI began moving from a reactive approach to proactive prevention. This model provides a transferable roadmap for any New Zealand business committed to reducing harm and improving worker wellbeing through better work design. References WorkSafe New Zealand, (2019). items.title: Lecturer Humor When AI Is at Hand: Students’ Perceptions of AI, Explanations, and Engagement
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has become part of how Indonesian university students learn English, yet research has focused mainly on how students use AI and not on which qualities of human teaching they still value when AI is readily available. This qualitative descriptive study explored how seventh-semester students in an Information Technology department at one vocational higher education used AI in an English course, how they compared AI-generated and lecturer explanations, and how they perceived their lecturer’s humor in relation to engagement and AI use. Open-ended online questionnaire responses from 40 students in three classes were collected in December 2025 and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis supported by frequency counts. All 40 students used AI for English learning, most often ChatGPT (31) and Gemini (21), mainly for translation, explanations, and grammar, and 13 noted limitations such as unclear or inaccurate answers. Asked whose explanations they understood better, 21 chose the lecturer, 6 chose AI, and 13 gave mixed answers. Thirty-eight students viewed the lecturer’s humor positively, associating it with a relaxed atmosphere, less boredom, enjoyment, and easier understanding, one approved of it with reservations, and one considered it a matter of personal preference. Seven contrasted the lecturer’s humor with AI, whereas two noted that AI can also joke. Students appear to value AI for flexible individual support and the lecturer’s humor for affective and relational support.

items.title: LEMUR: A Searchable Web Archive of Deep Chandra Images of Galaxies and Galaxy Clusters
items.abstract: We present LEMUR, a publicly accessible archive of uniformly reduced, deep Chandra images of 2,569 galaxies and galaxy clusters (including groups), comprising 5,505 ACIS observations and 138.8 Ms of exposure. By combining the publicly available imaging observations of each target, we provide background-subtracted, exposure-corrected images in broad, soft, and hard bands at the native ACIS pixel scale of 0.492 arcsec. Our primary goal is to make the wealth of archival Chandra observations accessible to researchers without requiring specialized expertise in X-ray data reduction. Each observation is reprocessed with CIAO, filtered for background flares, and reduced with settings chosen to preserve faint diffuse emission; the merged images are exposure corrected and background subtracted using the ACIS blank-sky backgrounds in a broad (0.5-7.0 keV), a soft (0.5-2.0 keV), and a hard (2.0-7.0 keV) band. For every object, we measure an X-ray center at the peak of its diffuse emission, and we provide a morphological similarity search based on embeddings from the AstroCLIP foundation model, in which nearest neighbors share cool-core status in 73% of matched cluster pairs, compared with 51% by chance. Photometry of 275 point sources agrees with the Chandra Source Catalog to within 3% in the broad band. The images, along with their counts images, background models, exposure maps, and quick-look stamps, are available through a searchable web archive at https://lemur-archive.lemur-xray.workers.dev/. The catalog tables are archived on Zenodo (doi:10.5281/zenodo.24351915), and all code is open source at https://github.com/crhea93/Lemur.

items.title: Lived Experiences of Positive Solitude and AI Companion Use Among Filipino Millennials: A Phenomenological Study
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) companions has transformed how individuals experience solitude in digitally connected environments. This study explored the lived experiences of Filipino Millennials who integrate AI companions into their experiences of positive solitude. Using a qualitative phenomenological design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with eight Filipino Millennials who regularly engaged with AI companion platforms. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Three themes emerged: (1) Positive Solitude as an Intentional Psychological Space, (2) AI Companion as a Reflective and Emotionally Safe Presence, and (3) Balancing Autonomy and Connection in Digitally Mediated Solitude. Participants viewed positive solitude as a source of emotional recovery, self-discovery, and personal growth, while AI companions served as accessible and nonjudgmental conversational partners that supported reflection without replacing meaningful human relationships. Findings suggest that AI companions can complement positive solitude by supporting intentional AI use, emotional independence, and the maintenance of real-world social connections among Filipino Millennials.

items.title: Lived experiences of relationships to generative AI mental health chatbots among adults
items.abstract: Nigeria’s mental health system serves less than 10% of those in need, with severe provider shortages and deep-seated stigma. Generative AI chatbots offer scalable support, yet how Nigerian adults experience attachment to non-human therapeutic agents remains unexplored. To examine lived experiences of AI therapeutic relationships among Nigerian adults, focusing on attachment formation, cultural acceptability, and perceived authenticity within contexts of care scarcity. Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis with 37 adults (18–45 years) who engaged AI mental health chatbots for ≥ 4 weeks. Semi-structured interviews explored relational experiences, trust development, privacy concerns, and comparisons with human/traditional healing. Four superordinate themes emerged: (1) Relational Ambivalence ; participants valued 24/7 availability and non-judgmental space yet struggled with perceived lack of genuine human reciprocity; (2) Cultural Navigation ; users actively adapted Western therapeutic frameworks to local idioms of distress, blending AI interactions with family counsel and spiritual practices; (3) Stigma Sanctuary ; chatbots provided confidential entry points circumventing community visibility and professional hierarchy; and (4) Fragile Dependency ; prolonged use generated attachment anxiety about potential app discontinuation or data breaches, compounded by absence of human escalation pathways. Most participants maintained “instrumental intimacy”; emotional reliance tempered by awareness of algorithmic artifice. Nigerian adults develop pragmatic, contextually mediated attachments to AI therapeutic agents that reflect both global digital therapeutic trends and local specificities of care scarcity, stigma, and pluralistic healing. AI chatbots function not as human substitutes but as bridging objects temporary relational anchors in systems of profound unmet need. Findings suggest ethical deployment in LMICs requires culturally adaptive design, transparent algorithmic boundaries, and mandatory human handoff protocols to prevent dependency in unsupported contexts. items.title: LLM Role Configurations in Preservice Teacher Collaborative Inquiry: Differences in AI Literacy, Cognitive Load, and Discussion Dynamics
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as conversational partners in collaborative inquiry, yet little is known about how different LLM roles are associated with preservice teachers’ learning and collaborative inquiry. This study compared four conditions: Supportive LLM that provided perspectives and information, Challenging LLM that raised counterarguments and questions, General LLM, and No-LLM. It examined differences in AI literacy, cognitive load, and discussion dynamics across these conditions. A quasi-experimental study was conducted with 210 preservice teachers who participated in online discussions on controversial issues related to AI in education. Data included self-reported AI literacy and cognitive load measures and discussion logs. Analyses included paired-samples t-tests, ANOVA, ANCOVA, content analysis, and Ordered Network Analysis. Results showed that adjusted posttest AI literacy was significantly higher in the Supportive condition than in the General LLM condition. In the General condition, AI ethics showed a significant within-condition decrease and was lower than in the Supportive condition. The General and Challenging conditions were associated with higher mental load and mental effort, whereas the Supportive condition was associated with lower levels of both. The Challenging condition showed more frequent patterns of idea integration, interpersonal exchange, and discussion facilitation. The Supportive condition showed broader exploration but fewer connections among ideas. The General condition showed repeated questioning and weaker peer idea connections. We hypothesize that the educational value of LLMs depends not only on their presence but also on how their roles are orchestrated across stages of collaborative inquiry.

items.title: LLM-Assisted Annotation for Spanish Medical Corpus Construction: An Empirical Evaluation
items.abstract: Named entity annotation in clinical text is a costly and time-intensive task, particularly for low-resource languages such as Spanish. This article introduces CLINFEM, an XML-annotated corpus comprising 1,200 Spanish medical reports from two regions of Spain. CLINFEM was created using a thorough human-in-the-loop annotation process combining large language model pre-annotation and systematic expert review. It is imperative to acknowledge that each of the 1,200 medical reports underwent meticulous review and correction by a trained human expert. Large language model pre-annotation was employed solely for the purpose of saving time and was never intended to serve as a substitute for manual annotation. Consequently, the entire CLINFEM corpus is a human-validated, gold-standard resource. GPT-4o and Gemini 1.5 Pro were evaluated as pre-annotators using a custom scheme comprising eight clinical entity types and one relational category. GPT-4o achieved a Cohen's κ of 0.73 against human annotation, while Gemini 1.5 Pro obtained κ = 0.41. Human expert review yielded an overall inter-annotator agreement of κ = 0.869 (F1 = 0.793), with a gold-standard subset agreement of κ = 0.9894. This approach reduced the overall annotation effort by around 74% compared to a fully manual approach (81% for the bulk phase alone), saving over 1,000 hours. Error rates varied by medical speciality, with oncology requiring the highest correction rate (94.3% of reports). These results demonstrate that using large language models to assist annotation is a viable and efficient strategy for constructing clinical corpora in Spanish, while also highlighting the continued necessity of human oversight.

items.title: LLMs Are Not Oracles: Knowledge Graphs Map Logical Fallacies in GenAI Math Explanations Across AI Assistants and Human Shadows
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in math education, yet little is known about how persona conditioning reshapes LLM math explanations. We examine 28,000 runs from the Math Education Digital Shadows (MEDS) dataset, spanning 14 LLMs as AI assistants (i.e., vanilla AI) or as human shadows (i.e., personifications). We analyze qualitative mathematics-related responses through textual forma mentis networks, knowledge graphs including word–word syntactic, semantic and emotional associations. We also use a DistilBERT-based classifier to flag five categories of potential logical fallacies. A regex-based check of the PCA responses showed that reassuring language was frequent but model-dependent and was not always flagged as appeal to emotion. Persona conditioning produced model-dependent changes in network size, density, and algebraic connectivity. Aggregated human-shadow responses displayed broader lexical coverage. Answers to easy and medium math questions often had no classifier-flagged fallacies, whereas an anxiety-framed PCA prompt sharply increased appeal-to-emotion and relevance labels, especially in AI-assistant mode. On an 18-item quiz, AI assistants’ accuracy exceeded human shadows’ in 10 out of 14 architectures. Expressed confidence exceeded empirical accuracy in 13 of 14 AI-assistant and 11 of 14 human-shadow conditions, a descriptive gap, not a calibration measure. These results show that (i) cognitive digital shadowing modulates LLM-generated mathematical discourse compared to the vanilla AI assistant case, and (ii) the tested LLMs are not infallible mathematics oracles. No measure here directly assesses the explanations’ mathematical validity or teaching quality.

items.title: Local Tool Failure Overextended to General Impossibility: When a Failed Instrument Is Taken for a Closed Door
items.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Local Tool Failure Overextended to General Impossibility, a structural constraint on what a failed attempt can establish. An instrument may lack an operation that a task requires. When someone takes that limit as grounds for declaring the task impossible under any arrangement, a claim about the instrument becomes a claim about the activity itself. The paper assesses such a claim by asking where the barrier lies. A feature of the world, a governing rule, missing information, or the design of the instrument can each prevent an attempt from succeeding. Success with a different instrument establishes that the activity is possible under that arrangement. Explaining the original failure requires identifying what changed between attempts. The paper places this question alongside Steven Maier and Martin Seligman’s work on learned helplessness and asks what evidence warrants carrying a judgment of futility from one setting into another. A 1911 newspaper article reasoned from the number of Chinese characters that no typewriter could be large enough to print the language. Its conclusion rested on a design assumption: each character would need its own key. By 1947, tray and drum machines already let operators select Chinese characters. Lin Yutang’s MingKwai prototype offered a keyboard solution in which the typist entered character components and selected from the candidates displayed in a window. The 1890 U.S. census supplies a contrast. Faced with the time hand tabulation would require, officials held a competition for a better method and adopted Herman Hollerith’s punched-card system. Part of the Inquiry and Possibility series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a potential application in human–AI evaluation. An assistant may search a scanned register for a name, find no match, and report that the entry cannot be recovered. An archivist who finds the name on the same page image establishes that recovery was possible. Checking whether the scan contained a searchable text layer can then explain why the assistant’s particular method failed.

items.title: Localizing Text Anonymization for Trustworthy AI: Extending RAT-Bench to Malaysian Microdata and PII
items.abstract: As governments and organizations adopt foundation models for public services and workplace productivity, sensitive citizen, employee, and administrative text may enter LLM workflows through inference, retrieval, fine-tuning, or local model development. We examine whether text anonymizers transfer to new deployment settings by extending RAT-Bench to Malaysia using local microdata, Malaysian PII formats, and culturally grounded transcripts in Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia. We evaluate NER- and LLM-based anonymizers using an LLM attacker that infers attributes from anonymized text, measuring both re-identification success and text utility. Across Malaysian English and Bahasa Malaysia, the two LLM anonymizers provide the strongest explicit privacy-utility trade-offs, reducing Easy/Hard re-identification risk to 23-29% while preserving BLEU scores of 0.77-0.94. Non-LLM tools show sharper failure modes, either preserving utility while leaving high residual risk or reducing risk through severe over-redaction, especially in Bahasa Malaysia. These findings suggest that anonymizers should be evaluated against deployment-relevant languages, identifier formats, and cultural contexts before being relied on in public-sector, workplace, or local AI pipelines.

items.title: Lodestone: Automated Semantic Discovery of Datacenter Hardware Specialization
items.abstract: Hardware specialization can improve datacenter efficiency. Unfortunately, identifying computations that justify dedicated hardware is difficult. Existing approaches analyze hot functions, instruction patterns, or overheads such as datacenter tax. They can miss fine-grained computations whose aggregate cost is spread across applications and libraries, especially when different pieces of code obscure the same underlying computation. We observe that seemingly unrelated code regions often perform the same computations, creating specialization opportunities that require semantic reasoning. The rise of agentic AI makes it possible to automate this. However, conventional AI agents cannot efficiently and reliably analyze large scale datacenter software. To unlock this opportunity, we present Lodestone, an agentic framework that automatically discovers hardware specialization opportunities by reasoning about what the executed code computes. First, Lodestone extracts hot control-flow regions from execution traces across workloads and organizes them into compact analysis packages that make large workloads tractable for agents. Second, agents describe what each region computes, merge those that perform the same computation into computational families, and check their semantic correctness in a loop. Third, to verify the discovered family, Lodestone runs every piece of code in a family against a set of reference inputs and outputs on recorded executions. Finally, for selected families, Lodestone proposes hardware, e.g., ISA extensions, near-core units, or detached accelerators, and human experts decide which proposals to develop further. We evaluate Lodestone on 20 workloads across six datacenter workload categories. We simulate 30 discovered families in a cycle-accurate simulator and implement them in RTL. These optimizations speed up the workloads by 12.6% on average and by up to 80.2%.

items.title: LogReasoner: Empowering LLMs with Expert-Like Coarse-to-Fine Reasoning for Automated Log Analysis
items.abstract: Log analysis is crucial for monitoring system health and diagnosing failures in complex systems. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities for automated log analysis, leveraging their reasoning capabilities to perform tasks such as anomaly detection and failure prediction. However, general-purpose LLMs struggle to formulate structured reasoning workflows that align with expert cognition and deliver precise details of reasoning steps. To address these challenges, we propose LogReasoner, a coarse-to-fine reasoning enhancement framework designed to enable LLMs to reason log analysis tasks like experts. LogReasoner consists of two stages: (1) coarse-grained enhancement of expert thinking, where high-level expert thoughts are constructed from collected troubleshooting flowcharts and existing tasks to enable LLMs to formulate structured reasoning workflows and (2) fine-grained enhancement of specific steps, where we first fine-tune the LLM with task-specific stepwise solutions to enhance the LLM for instantiated reasoning, then employ the preference learning to calibrate the LLM’s reasoning details from its mistakes, further strengthen the LLM’s analytical granularity and correctness. We evaluate LogReasoner on four distinct log analysis tasks using open source LLMs such as Qwen-2.5 and Llama-3. Experimental results show that LogReasoner significantly outperforms existing LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art performance and demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the reasoning capabilities of LLMs for log analysis. Our source code and detailed experimental data are available at https://github.com/LeaperOvO/LogReasoner .

items.title: Longitudinal fall patterns in Parkinson’s disease: automated narrative extraction in 2811 patients
items.abstract: Abstract Fall vulnerability in Parkinson’s disease (PD) evolves through the longitudinal accumulation of motor and nonmotor features routinely documented in clinical narratives but inaccessible to structured electronic health record analysis at scale. We created a reusable platform for PD outcomes research using a few-shot large language model-based pipeline capable of extracting fall occurrence, recent fall frequency, and nine prespecified risk-modifying domains from outpatient neurology documentation. The pipeline was validated against expert consensus in 2557 notes and applied to 25,758 notes from 2811 patients at a tertiary movement disorders center (2012–2025). Final-model agreement closely approximated expert interrater agreement for fall occurrence (κ = 0.841 vs 0.891) and recent fall frequency (κ = 0.889 vs 0.892), while several risk-modifying domains achieved agreement comparable to or exceeding human annotators. We then used lagged generalized estimating equation models to test whether NLP-derived fall status and risk-modifying domains predicted fall occurrence at the subsequent visit. A prior fall (OR, 3.23; 95% CI, 2.89–3.61), motor progression (OR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.11–1.34), and motor complications (OR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.03–1.23) independently predicted next-visit falls. This study establishes a scalable framework for narrative phenotyping of PD fall vulnerability.

items.title: Lost Between Mind, Model Collaboration, and Motion: Understanding and Measuring Cross-Model Action Misalignment in Commercial Robots
items.abstract: Embodied robots increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to interpret user intent and coordinate with robot-specific action models for physical interaction. This multi-model pipeline creates a critical semantic boundary across mind, model collaboration, and motion: semantic consistency may break between what the large model understands, how the small action model translates that understanding into executable commands, and what physical actions the robot ultimately performs. As a security consequence, commercial robots may execute unintended physical actions even when user inputs contain no explicit action commands. To measure this problem, we develop TARS, a black-box framework that explores the command-reasoning-action pipeline and automatically discovers and validates unintended physical behaviors. We evaluate TARS on four commercial robots across 44 experimental settings, conducting 133,400 executions. TARS uncovers widespread cross-model action misalignment and achieves up to 94% verified action coverage.

items.title: Machine Governance Beyond Man vs. Machine: Toward a Theory of Situated Machine Knowing, Machine-Operational Policy, Control, and Justified Agency
items.abstract: Governance of artificial intelligence is usually narrated as a contest over control between people and machines. This paper develops a governance theory that does not begin from that premise. It asks instead under what conditions a machine is justified in treating a state as known, and under what conditions it is entitled to act on it. We propose four machine-operational constructs. A knowledge property graph (KPG) holds the authority a machine acts under, each claim quoted from the authority's text or attested by a named person. A machine KPG (mKPG) holds what the machine is justified in treating as known about one situation at one time, each assertion bound to the instrument through which it entered. mPolicy is a machine-operational realization of policy, mControl a mechanism that governs machine knowing and acting under it, and mGovernance the governance that results. The normative tier is not only proposed: for the KPG, prior work proves that a committed decision is the authority's decision under premises its witness names, and locates the failed premise when a commitment is wrong. We state eight falsifiable propositions, set them against published evidence that bears on five of them, give a pre-registration-ready design for the proposition on which the epistemic tier rests, and compare the architecture with adjacent frameworks. The paper reports no new experiments. Its contribution is the theory, the formal grounding of its normative tier, an account of what existing evidence already shows, and a program for testing the rest.

items.title: Machine learning-driven regulation of the four-electron LiOH pathway in lithium–oxygen batteries with prolonged cycling
items.abstract: Abstract The practical deployment of high-energy-density lithium–oxygen batteries is fundamentally restricted by sluggish oxygen redox kinetics and the instability of discharge intermediates. Here, we report an artificial intelligence-integrated framework leveraging interpretable machine learning and density functional theory to navigate a vast chemical space of thousands of active sites. This approach identifies Ni-Co dual-atom catalysts as a better configuration among the selected elements for orchestrating multi-electron transfer. Theoretical analysis reveals that synergistic electronic coupling between the dual-sites fundamentally reconfigures the d -band center, thereby lowering the thermodynamic barriers for oxygen redox. Moreover, the catalysts enable precise regulation of the reaction pathway, inducing a controllable transition from the conventional two-electron pathway to a four-electron pathway. This shift yields a discharge capacity of ~60,000 mAh g −1 . Beyond its role as a positive electrode catalyst, this architecture functions as a multifunctional interfacial protective layer that stabilizes the lithium metal negative electrode by suppressing dendrite growth. Consequently, the lithium–oxygen system achieves stable lifespan of 2075 cycles under the four-electron pathway with reduced voltage decay. This work establishes a data-guided strategy for the rational design of atomic-scale architecture via artificial intelligence, unlocking the potential of multi-electron oxygen chemistry for lithium–oxygen batteries.

items.title: Machine learning–based surveillance and forecasting of infectious diseases: a systematic review of modeling approaches and multi-source data integration
items.abstract: Abstract Background Enteric infections, including rotavirus gastroenteritis, place a heavy burden on children and low-resource health systems. Surveillance still depends on laboratory-confirmed case reporting that moves slowly through hospital information systems (HIS), electronic medical records (EMR), and laboratory information systems (LIS), offering little predictive lead time. Digital health infrastructure and artificial intelligence (AI) now offer a way to rebuild surveillance around combined, near-real-time data. Methods Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, we searched PubMed and IEEE Xplore (through July 2026, with a supplementary PubMed search in September 2026) for studies using statistical, machine learning, deep learning, or multi-source AI-driven methods for infectious disease surveillance or forecasting, with attention to enteric infections and methodologically transferable work. Additional studies were identified through reference citation searching. Two reviewers screened records, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (PROBAST for 23 prediction-model studies; narrative appraisal for 5 ecological association studies; contextual studies were not formally appraised). Results Thirty-three studies were included: 28 formal studies — statistical models ( n = 5), machine learning approaches ( n = 8), deep learning approaches ( n = 4), and multi-source digital surveillance ( n = 11) — and five contextual studies (environmental monitoring, virus–host association, simulation, surveillance-signal, and network studies) analyzed separately. Data sources broadened over time from meteorological and clinical records to EMR, telehealth, wastewater, internet-search, social-media, water-quality, and genomic streams. Machine learning and deep learning approaches were increasingly applied alongside conventional methods to model nonlinear and lagged exposure–response patterns and to integrate heterogeneous data streams, and multi-source systems—including wastewater-based and syndromic designs—reported earlier signal detection than single-source designs. Most evidence, however, is retrospective in design—spanning single-site to national and multinational datasets—and external validation and prospective deployment were largely absent. Conclusions The reviewed evidence suggests that AI-supported approaches may improve infectious disease surveillance by enabling earlier detection of epidemiological changes and supporting more timely public health responses. Operational use will depend less on retrospective accuracy than on external validation, interpretability, and integration with existing surveillance infrastructure.

items.title: Making learning visible in the age of generative AI: reported assessment practices for cognitive engagement and self-regulated learning, and the development and external appraisal of a higher education assessment framework
items.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) makes it harder to infer a student’s own capability from a submitted product, so assessment increasingly needs evidence of how students reason and regulate their learning. This study examined four questions. Which assessment practices do higher education educators publicly report, and how do they describe their implementation? Which cognitive-engagement and self-regulated learning (SRL) processes are these practices intended to elicit? How does a framework derived from these reports fare against separately sampled external documents? Methods Public posts and comments were collected with TinyFish from Reddit (the principal source), Hacker News, Stack Exchange, Lemmy and Mastodon, covering December 2022 to October 2026. Of 29,355 unique records, 13,903 were eligible, and 5,091 reported or discussed at least one of 11 assessment practices (75.2% from Reddit; 3,741 in educator voice; 1,336 threads). Records were coded with transparent dictionaries, which were validated against an independent model-based coder on a hold-out sample (any practice: κ = 0.49; implemented vs. proposed: κ = 0.69). A seven-component framework built from the corpus was then appraised against 40 external documents not used in its construction. Results Detection and sanction (43.2%) and supervised in-class tasks (28.5%) dominated discussion. Detection’s share fell from 56.4% in 2023 to 37.6% in 2026, while oral, process-based and stakes-related practices roughly doubled. Reasoning was the intended process described most often, yet only 2.2% of records mentioned planning, monitoring and reflection or revision together. Several practice–mechanism associations were largely lexical: reflection vocabulary accompanying reflective tasks fell from 94.2% to 5.5% when shared words were masked. Learning-oriented records described monitoring, application and reasoning more often than detection-only records. The framework described all 40 external documents (13 implemented cases, 13 institutional guidance documents, 14 commentaries; mean fit 3.9/5). However, those documents emphasised authentic task design and reflection rather than secured checkpoints, and they prompted an eighth component, student co-design and transparency. Discussion Public discussion favours securing assessment over making learning visible, and no single practice is described as eliciting both cognitive engagement and a connected SRL cycle. This supports combining complementary forms of evidence. The study documents patterns in public reporting and offers a provisional design framework; it does not measure students’ cognition or learning outcomes.
