items.title: Mapping artificial intelligence for science with open metadata reveals shifting evidence regimes across scientific domains
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence for science (AI4S) is often discussed as a unified transformation, although scientific domains differ markedly in how model outputs are tested, validated, and justified. We map an audited corpus of N=2,784 records (2014–2025) retrieved from Crossref and screened with a frozen, versioned rulebook, and compare evidence regimes in protein science, materials design, drug discovery, closed-loop experimentation, and mathematical reasoning. Using term co-occurrence, reference co-citation, burst detection, growth models, and collaboration networks, we identify three robust patterns: (i) rapid but decelerating growth (Poisson rate 1.381, 95% CI 1.361–1.402, declining from 1.537 in 2014–2019 to 1.320 in 2019–2025); (ii) a coherent term-co-occurrence structure (75 nodes, modularity Q=0.404 ) organized around four measured streams—representation learning, generative and inverse design, closed-loop experimentation, and neuro-symbolic reasoning—with the generative stream acting as the connecting hub; and (iii) a right-boundary rise in large language model terminology (burst state 3) that a year-by-year backtest shows is not a last-observation artefact. The maps are sensitive to metadata availability: abstract coverage is 50.6%, reference coverage 84.3%, and a title-only variant changes the network partition substantially (adjusted Rand index 0.762), so the maps describe the screened open-metadata corpus rather than the total AI4S literature. Cross-domain analysis shows that AI most consequentially shifts scientific bottlenecks from representation and candidate generation toward experimental or formal validation, provenance, and responsibility for claims. We contribute an auditable, open-metadata science-mapping workflow designed for reproducibility and an evidence-regime framework for analysing how epistemic labour is redistributed across models, instruments, formal verifiers, infrastructures, and human experts.

items.title: MARS Technical Report
items.abstract: Modern industrial recommender systems use multi-stage cascades--retrieval, pre-ranking, ranking, and re-ranking--to narrow millions of candidates to a personalized list. While each stage deploys sophisticated models, pipeline-level decisions on channel activation, quotas, model selection, and score fusion remain engineer-tuned and user-agnostic within each scenario. This report presents MARS (Multi-stage Agentic Recommendation System), extending personalization from individual-stage predictions to full pipeline orchestration. A near-line agent built on fine-tuned Qwen3-0.6B generates per-user configurations--a seven-dimensional action covering pipeline mode, retrieval quotas, model selection, fusion weights, and reranker settings--from a constrained action space. Configurations are validated, cached, and consumed asynchronously; the cascade never waits for LLM inference. Schema checks, fallbacks, and a kill switch ensure serving safety. The policy is trained in three stages: Confidence-aware SFT distills schema-valid generation from a teacher model; Format-Anchored Preference Optimization (FAPO) learns action preferences via ActionMask with posterior weighting; Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) refines the policy through Sandbox replay with a frozen reward model, without exposing exploratory actions to live traffic. Two-week A/B tests across five Taobao scenarios with over ten million daily users show positive gains on all key metrics. The largest reach +5.22% V2P and +7.34% GMV, with positive CTR lifts on both click surfaces. About 20% of requests use a lightweight Minimal mode, and deployment shows 12 ms lower mean serving latency versus production.

items.title: Mathematics Teacher Interaction Styles with Generative Artificial Intelligence: Personalization in Word- Problem Design
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) plays an increasing role in K-12 mathematics classrooms, understanding how teachers collaborate with these technologies during instructional design is essential. Drawing on frameworks related to personalization theory, Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge, and adaptive epistemic agency, this study examined how seven seventh-grade mathematics teachers interacted with ChatGPT to personalize mathematics word problems to students’ interests. Analyses of teacher-GenAI interactions identified three interaction styles: AI-Dominated-Passive Prompt Personalization, Teacher-Dominated-Rigid Personalization, and Human-AI partnership-Collaborative Personalization. Students' ratings of the resulting personalized problems varied across teachers and interaction styles, with the strongest positive patterns occurring among teachers characterized by Collaborative Personalization. Collaborative personalization illustrates how teachers may maintain epistemic authority for evaluating mathematical, pedagogical, and contextual appropriateness while selectively granting GenAI generative authority to expand personalization possibilities. These findings highlight the importance of preparing teachers to critically evaluate and collaboratively engage with GenAI during instructional design.

items.title: Mechanistic Critics for Sample-Efficient NPU Design-Space Exploration
items.abstract: NPU design-space exploration for LLM inference mainly relies on an expensive simulator that often returns only scalar feedback such as latency and power. Such feedback can rank evaluated configurations, but gives little information for deciding why a configuration is slow or which architecture parameter should be changed next. This limitation is especially severe because prefill and decode workloads can be limited by different resources, including compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. We propose CriticNPU, a sample-efficient DSE framework built around an online-calibrated mechanistic critic for NPU architecture design. The critic uses explicit hardware limits to evaluate NPU configurations: before simulation, it estimates whether a proposed configuration is likely to improve over the current best and filters weak candidates; after simulation, it aggregates operator-level runtimes into prefill/decode bottleneck summaries and predicts the effect of candidate parameter changes. We instantiate the critic with a Roofline-style model that derives compute and memory limits from architecture parameters and calibrates per-operator-type effective limits using simulator observations. And CriticNPU combines this critic with a workload extractor and an architecture planner to propose configurations. Across six LLM workloads and 16 deployment configurations per model, CriticNPU achieves best-or-tied-best latency in 74% of prefill and 87.5% of decode settings while using roughly half the simulator calls of competitive DSE baselines. We conduct extensive ablation studies and detailed analyses to validate the effectiveness of our method from multiple perspectives. Our code is available at https://github.com/bruno686/CriticNPU.

items.title: Mechanomedicine for Lung Transplantation: From Multiscale Forces to AI‐Assisted Translation
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Long‐term outcomes after lung transplantation remain limited by primary graft dysfunction and chronic lung allograft dysfunction, despite improvements in surgery, immunosuppression and infection control. Mechanical injury is a complementary contributor that remains insufficiently integrated into transplant care. The lung allograft must accommodate cyclic ventilation, reperfusion shear, thoracic constraints and matrix remodeling. These forces can disrupt the alveolar‐capillary barrier, amplify inflammation and activate fibrotic programmes. Here we synthesize lung transplantation through a mechanomedicine framework that links organ‐scale loading, cellular mechanotransduction and clinical decision‐making. We discuss how computational models and artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate ex vivo lung perfusion waveforms, imaging‐derived ventilation or strain patterns, and molecular injury markers to support graft‐risk assessment. We then organize mechanotherapeutic strategies by clinical readiness, from protective ventilation, size matching and extracorporeal graft support to emerging interventions targeting mechanotransduction according to cell type and loading conditions. Finally, we outline a translational roadmap for standardized mechanical biomarkers, interpretable AI and clinician‐supervised digital‐twin models.

items.title: MEM-STRESS: Longitudinal Field Study of a Wearable-Informed AI Chatbot for Stress Management
items.abstract: Stress is an increasingly prevalent concern, creating a need for accessible and personalized support. Stress-management chatbots primarily rely on what users report, which may not capture their physiological changes. Wearables capture these changes, but chatbots rarely use them as memory across conversations. We therefore present MEM-STRESS, a stress-support chatbot that turns a wearable ring's physiological data into a layered memory of daily records, baseline deviations, LLM-generated summaries, and uses it to drive multi-session conversations grounded in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT). In a four-week, non-randomized study with 60 adults, we compared MEM-STRESS (Treatment) with a chatbot remembering only past conversations (Control). Memory shaped the conversations: The Treatment chatbot referenced participants' physiological features (e.g., activity in 71.8% of sessions) and suggested more body-related DBT skills than Control (14.5% vs. 5.7%), with Treatment participants also using slightly more body-related words (1.76% vs. 1.45%). Treatment participants praised personalization three times as often (44.4% vs. 14.3%), more frequently reported reflecting differently on stress (69.0% vs. 46.4%, not significant), and described gaining insight into their stress signals. Their perceived stress fell 14.2% from baseline versus 3.6% for Control, though the group difference was not significant. Grounding stress-support chatbots in layered physiological memory is thus feasible and may improve perceived personalization, motivating larger randomized studies.

items.title: MENTORA: AN INTELLIGENT AI-DRIVEN FRAMEWORK FOR ACADEMIC WORKFLOW AUTOMATION AND OUTCOME-BASED EDUCATION MANAGEMENT
items.abstract: This paper presents MENTORA, an intelligent AI-driven framework designed to automate and centralize faculty-oriented academic workflows in higher education institutions. The proposed platform integrates academic planning, syllabus progress tracking, timetable management, student roster management, attendance monitoring, assessment preparation, course outcome mapping, and faculty assistance within a unified application. MENTORA is developed using Python, Flask, Flask-Login, Flask-SQLAlchemy, PostgreSQL, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Bootstrap. It incorporates Google's Gemini models for multimodal timetable and student roster information extraction, as well as AI-assisted faculty support and assessment content generation. Scikit-learn is used for question classification based on Bloom's taxonomy and difficulty levels, while TF-IDF similarity supports course outcome mapping and duplicate question detection. The framework follows a hybrid AI architecture that combines generative AI, conventional machine learning, text similarity analysis, and rule-based processing while retaining faculty oversight for important academic decisions. This paper describes the problem context, related work, objectives, system architecture, functional modules, implementation technologies, workflow design, security considerations, and a proposed evaluation methodology. Quantitative performance results and expert validation are not reported in this manuscript; these remain subjects for future empirical evaluation. Keywords: Academic workflow automation, Artificial Intelligence, Generative AI, Higher Education, Machine Learning, Bloom's Taxonomy, Outcome-Based Education.

items.title: MetacouplingLLM: Integrating geographic adjacency, flow indicators, and LLM-assisted analysis
items.abstract: The metacoupling framework examines interactions within coupled human and natural systems and between adjacent or distant systems, but its application is constrained by inconsistent geographic classifications and limited standardized quantitative workflows. We present MetacouplingLLM, an open-source Python package integrating adjacency databases, reproducible flow indicators, and large language model (LLM)-assisted qualitative analysis. The databases combine administrative boundaries, hydrography, and fixed-crossing evidence, with configurable adjacency policies and optional country-level maritime adjacency. Metacoupled Flow Shares, Metacoupled Flow Evenness, and the Metacoupled Flow Concentration Index characterize flow composition, balance across coupling types, and partner concentration within each type. The qualitative workflow combines literature retrieval, optional web evidence, and geographic checks to draft structured analyses. Applications to global marine fishing and Indonesian palm oil demonstrate these capabilities; the fisheries reanalysis reveals differing partner concentration among regions with similar telecoupled flow shares. MetacouplingLLM facilitates consistent framework application and comparative sustainability research.

items.title: Metadata-Driven AI: An Architectural Pattern for Sustainable Data Analysis with LLMs
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) let users analyse data in natural language, either by giving the data to the model to read directly or by having the model generate code to process it. Both routes send the data, or fragments of it, to the model; both pay for inference on every run; and the code a model writes to answer a question is usually discarded once the question is answered. We present Metadata-Driven AI, an architectural pattern that keeps the data away from the model and turns each analysis into a reusable program. Only metadata (not the actual data) crosses a one-way inference boundary to the LLM. The program the LLM returns runs next to the data and is kept, so that inference is paid once per analysis rather than once per run. We describe the pattern together with a simple cost model, a measurement of how little information crosses the boundary on public datasets, and a benchmark showing that a small, locally hosted model can serve as the generator. We illustrate the pattern on three applications, each built on a different implementation of it: geospatial photovoltaic prospection over live public APIs, extraction of portfolio positions from bank statements, and a conversational assistant over smart-city dashboards.

items.title: MIRAGE: A Framework for Multi-hop Reasoning under Dynamic Knowledge Injection
items.abstract: Multi-hop Question Answering (MQA) requires large language models (LLMs) to retrieve and synthesize multiple pieces of evidence into a coherent reasoning path, which is essential for complex tasks. However, prior work on knowledge updating for MQA has largely focused on simple fact edits, overlooking a more challenging and realistic setting---\emph{Knowledge Injection}---in which the model must simultaneously accommodate both conflicting updates and entirely novel information. Under this setting, a hop-level answer is often wrong simply because the model trusts the wrong knowledge source: it clings to outdated parametric memory when the injected knowledge conflicts with it (K2), and it cannot answer when the required fact is entirely new (K3). To investigate this, we introduce NEXUS, the first benchmark tailored for multi-hop reasoning under Knowledge Injection, which explicitly covers both conflicting (K2) and incremental (K3) knowledge. We further propose MIRAGE, an efficient, training-free framework whose core component, the Correlation-aware Dual-path Reasoner (CDR), resolves such per-hop source-trust errors via P(True)-based confidence routing, complemented by a lightweight template-guided corrector for residual structural deviations. Extensive experiments across four LLM families and two benchmarks demonstrate that MIRAGE consistently improves both final-answer accuracy and hop-level reasoning accuracy, establishing a new state of the art in this challenging setting.

items.title: MLE Agents: Autonomous ML Engineering in Large-scale Recommendation Systems
items.abstract: The typical workflow for improving large-scale ranking and recommendation models is slow and tedious: an engineer forms a hypothesis, implements it as a code change, trains a model, and evaluates it both offline and online, often relying on their own intuition and experience along the way. Autonomous LLM agents promise to speed this up by running the loop on their own, but it is still unclear whether they can do this in industry-scale systems rather than on benchmarks or small proxy tasks. We build human-on-the-loop machine learning engineer (MLE) agents that propose, implement, train, and evaluate model changes on large-scale search rankers. Engineers retain control over objective design, search direction, and final-model review. We identify three obstacles that make this industry setting challenging: feedback takes hours per experiment, offline metrics do not always predict online impact, and improvements saturate after the early wins. We address these with parallel training runs, an objective calibrated to match online impact, and careful context engineering. In one campaign, the system ran 1,097 completed candidate experiments and accepted 325, a 29.6\% acceptance rate compared with 15.6\% in the earlier campaign under a different objective and search constraint. Its best model increases search volume by 0.23\% in an A/B test of large scale. Several improvements were architectural changes the team had never tried, drawn from the broader industry and literature, suggesting that MLE agents can explore regions of the design space that human intuition overlooks. We find that the design of the harness around the model matters: intuition suggests that a stronger underlying model is enough, but in our experience, the design of the loop around it is just as critical. More broadly, our work shows that autonomous agents can do real machine-learning engineering in industry-scale systems.

items.title: Modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa para promover el pensamiento crítico y el aprendizaje significativo en educación media colombiana
items.abstract: La incorporación de inteligencia artificial generativa en la educación media plantea una tensión entre su potencial de apoyo y el riesgo de sustituir procesos cognitivos esenciales. El objetivo de este estudio fue diseñar un modelo pedagógico mediado por inteligencia artificial generativa que promueva pensamiento crítico y aprendizaje significativo en estudiantes de educación media colombiana, bajo una perspectiva humanocéntrica de Sociedad 5.0. Se desarrolló una investigación cualitativa, documental, interpretativa y teórico-propositiva. El corpus estuvo compuesto por 40 fuentes: 35 sustantivas y cinco metodológicas, examinadas mediante ocho categorías y una ruta de diez fases. La síntesis produjo ocho hallazgos documentales y sustentó CRISOL-IA 5.0, integrado por diez principios, siete componentes y seis fases: Contextualizar, Recuperar, Interrogar, Someter a contraste, Organizar y Lograr transferencia. Su funcionamiento se representó en una secuencia demostrativa de cuatro sesiones para grado décimo, con seis evidencias observables. La comprobación conceptual mostró cobertura de las seis fases y los siete componentes; de nueve criterios funcionales, seis se cumplieron en el diseño, dos quedaron condicionados por el contexto institucional y uno —eficacia educativa— requiere aplicación con participantes. Se concluye que el aporte ofrece una arquitectura pedagógica trazable y adaptable, sin constituir todavía una validación empírica.

items.title: Modern Digital Tools for Monitoring the Implementation of Strategic Program Documents of the Russian Federation
items.abstract: The article examines digital monitoring of the implementation of strategic program documents of the Russian Federation and its connection to the evaluation of political and administrative decisions. It aims to identify the functions of modern information tools and the conditions for the managerial suitability of the data they gener-ate. The methods employed include normative analysis, functional comparison of government information systems, and qualitative document analysis. The research materials comprise legal acts, official publications of the Federal Treasury, and scholarly papers on public administration. Monitoring practices described in 2024 are compared with institutional changes introduced in 2026. The article identifies the distribution of functions be-tween the State Automated System “Upravlenie”, the State Integrated Information System “Electronic Budget”, and the state statistical platform within the unified plan for achieving national goals. It establishes the im-portance of accounting for the relationships between activities, indicators and national goal components, pre-serving the revision history, and documenting corrective action. The article proposes an analytical monitoring record, along with six criteria for the managerial suitability of monitoring, covering goal alignment, evidential support, temporal comparability, revision history, cross-system comparability, and completeness of response. The article also explores the conditions for verifying relationships and predictive signals derived with the use of artificial intelligence. The paper concludes that digital tools should be studied together with procedures for building evidence and using information within the competences of management participants.

items.title: Monitoring Unplanned Construction Using Satellite Change Detection
items.abstract: Cities need land for homes, shops, roads, and public services. New construction changes that land. It can harm natural areas and water bodies, add to waste, and strain public services. NITI Aayog's 2021 report stated that 65% of 7,933 urban settlements in India had no master plan. That number tells us about planning coverage at the time. It does not tell us whether any single building was authorised. Artificial intelligence, which lets computers learn patterns from data, can help find physical changes by comparing satellite images taken on different dates. We test simple methods on two public datasets from outside India. First, we turn each image into a set of numbers using a pretrained neural network, a model already trained to recognise patterns in images. We feed those numbers to standard machine-learning classifiers that predict land categories and physical changes. The methods reach about 95 percent accuracy at spotting built-up land and about 83 percent accuracy at saying whether a small pair of images shows change, where each pair gets one label. We also train a small neural network on a standard change-detection benchmark. Separately, we run a preliminary descriptive check on an Agra sample of 48 patches, 7 of them positive. The results show that satellite images carry information about physical change. They do not show whether construction was planned or permitted.

items.title: Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA) for Plant Spectroscopy
items.abstract: Plant reflectance spectroscopy across the visible, near-infrared, and shortwave infrared domain encodes foliar biochemical and anatomical traits into contiguous spectral signatures with locally differentiable structure; however, extreme inter-band collinearity and unfavorable sample-to-feature ratios challenge predictive modeling. Conventional dimensionality reduction methods routinely adopted in spectroscopy, are column-permutation invariant: they treat adjacent wavelengths as unordered tabular columns and discard the sequential differential geometry of absorption features. Here, we propose Morpho-Spectral Projection Analysis (MSPA), a supervised dimensionality reduction operator that projects contiguous spectra into a compact morpho-spectral subspace through three complementary blocks: (i) additive continuum-removed absorption depth, area, and red-edge inflection kinematics; (ii) local multi-order singular eigenmodes (0th, 1st, and 2nd derivatives) partitioned across contiguous radiative sub-windows; and (iii) global Fisher-weighted canonical subspaces regularized via trace-normalized isotropic covariance shrinkage. We validated MSPA across 8,963 spectra spanning five plant systems, coupled with six classical machine learning classifiers and four Tabular Foundation Models (TabPFN v3, TabICL v2, TabDPT v1.2, and TabFM). Despite compressing the 1,580-band spectrum by 96%, MSPA outperformed the full spectrum in 92.0% of all benchmarks and conventional reducers in 90.0% of all model-crop evaluations, raising the global mean macro-F1 from 0.7756 (full spectrum) to 0.8520, accelerating in-context inference by up to 126.5x. Designed as a self-contained spectral projection operator, the MSPA method can be directly integrated into spectroscopy workflows via the open-source code available at GitHub: https://github.com/Lucas-Osco/mspa.

items.title: Multifunctional Nanomaterial-Based Electrochemical Biosensors for Disease Monitoring and Therapeutic Assessment
items.abstract: As the prevalence of chronic and communicable diseases increases, there has been an enhanced need for sensitive, rapid, reliable, and minimally invasive diagnostic technologies for monitoring disease progression and therapeutic effectiveness. Multifunctional nanomaterial-based electrochemical biosensors are emerging as powerful analytical tools due to their high sensitivity, selectivity, portability, and potential for real-time biomolecule detection. The purpose of this review is to shed light on the key underlying principles, nanomaterial engineering strategies, sensing principles, medical applications, and therapeutic assessment functionality of advanced electrochemical biosensors. Throughout the review, the merits of metallic nanoparticles, metal oxides, carbon nanotubes, graphene, MXenes, metal-organic frameworks, conducting polymers, and hybrid nanomaterials in increasing electrode conductivity, electroactive surface area, biomolecule immobilization, electron transfer kinetic, and electrochemical signal enhancement will be highlighted. This review delves deeper into the potential uses of sensors in identifying and tracking the processes of cancer, diseases of the cardiovascular system, diabetes, infections, problems in the nervous system, and cases of inflammation. It thoroughly discusses the role of drug monitoring, pharmacokinetics, and the potential uses of electrochemical sensors in providing ongoing monitoring of drugs in the human body. In addition, advancements in devices that are wearable and implantable, implement multiplexing, microfluidic principles, and artificial intelligence in biosensing are considered in the aspect of personal health and health care. Despite a multitude of technological improvements still present issues of biofouling, toxicity of nanomaterial, stability of biosensors, reproducibility, interference, calibration, mass production, and certification which makes it impossible to translate it into the practices of functional medicine.

items.title: Multiple disease detection and prediction using advanced computing technologies: a comprehensive systematic review
items.abstract: Multimorbidity—the concurrent presence of two or more chronic long-term conditions—affects more than 37% of the global adult population and consumes 55%–80% of healthcare expenditure in high-income systems, yet artificial intelligence (AI) diagnostic systems remain overwhelmingly disease-specific, creating a profound structural mismatch with the multi-disease complexity characterizing the majority of real-world clinical encounters across twelve review-defined disease groups mapped to World Health Organization (WHO) ICD-11 chapters. This systematic review, following PRISMA 2020 and registered with OSF.IO (Registration DOI number: 10.17605/OSF.IO/3HZ45; Date of Registration: 25 October 2026), evaluated advanced AI technologies for simultaneous multi-domain disease detection and prediction. Nine electronic databases, PubMed/MEDLINE, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, Springer Link, Wiley, MDPI, and Google Scholar, were searched for peer-reviewed literature published from January 2015 to 31 August 2026. Database-specific Boolean searches (full strings in Supplementary Table S1 ) combined AI terms with terms for the twelve review-defined disease groups. Quality appraisal was done using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST tools (Cohen's κ = 0.84 refers to study screening agreement). Of 4,215 records identified (3,368 after removing 847 duplicates; 612 full texts assessed; 332 excluded), 280 studies met the eligibility criteria and were included in the qualitative synthesis, and 185 provided quantitative performance data for a descriptive (non-pooled) synthesis. Deep learning models such as CNN, LSTM, ViT, and GNN reported high but heterogeneous discrimination across the twelve disease groups (AUC: 0.85–0.991). These values come from different tasks, datasets, and validation designs; they are not pooled estimates and do not show superiority of any architecture. Three of the highest-reporting single-disease studies (retrospective and not directly comparable) include: diabetic retinopathy detection (AUC 0.991; n = 128,175); cancer whole-slide image classification (AUC 0.98; n = 44,732); and cardiac arrhythmia detection (AUC 0.97; n = 91,232 ECGs). Convolutional neural networks were the most popular network type (26% of studies), while the main programming language was Python (68%). Three repeated gaps can be seen in the field of research in general, and those are: 1) lack of representation of people from developing countries in the training data; 2) scarce evidence from randomized prospective trials showing improved patient outcomes; and 3) an underdeveloped regulatory pathway for multi-disease AI as Software as a Medical Device (SaMD). Realizing simultaneous multi-disease AI at clinical scale demands five coordinated priorities: standardized cross-category benchmarks, demographically inclusive datasets with mandatory low- and middle-income country representation, prospective randomized trial validation, federated privacy-enhancing infrastructure designed to support GDPR, HIPAA, and DPDPA 2023 compliance (federated learning alone does not establish compliance), and internationally harmonized regulatory governance for multi-disease Software as a Medical Device authorization. Limitations of the review itself (English-only restriction, heterogeneity, overlapping public datasets, publication bias) are discussed in Section 8.5 . items.title: Narrative Threat Zine-ing: Storytelling and Reproductive Privacy Communication
items.abstract: The U.S. reproductive health landscape is fragmented, with legal, digital, and interpersonal privacy risks that are highly contextual and often poorly addressed by conventional privacy guidance. Prior work has proposed narrative threat modeling as an alternative to predominantly technical approaches to reproductive privacy communication. Building on this work, we introduce narrative threat zine-ing , a qualitative method that invites participants to communicate reproductive privacy through story and form rather than checklists or technical instruction. We report findings from four zine-making workshops in which participants created zines for people they worried about in the post- Roe landscape. Participants consistently framed reproductive privacy through relationships, lived experience, and storytelling, positioning zines as tools for awareness, solidarity, and collective sensemaking rather than prescriptive guidance. We argue that narrative threat zine-ing offers a method for examining how people interpret and communicate reproductive privacy under conditions of legal and social uncertainty.

items.title: NatBDI: Combining BDI reasoning and natural language inference for autonomous agents
items.abstract: Developing autonomous agents to deal with real-world problems is challenging, especially when developers are not necessarily specialists in artificial intelligence. Recent advances in machine learning for natural language processing tasks are reaching performance levels suitable for practical applications, although these approaches rely on opaque, inscrutable models. This poses three key challenges: the interface between the programming and the developer, the efficiency of the resulting agents, and the scrutiny of their behaviour. We tackle the challenge of developing autonomous agents over natural language environments in an efficient agent architecture that leverages recent developments in natural language processing and the intuitive folk psychology abstraction of the beliefs, desires, intentions (BDI) architecture. This paper introduces NatBDI , a new class of agent architecture that uses the BDI reasoning cycle with components driven by natural language processing. This allows a developer to instruct the agent more directly using a combination of controlled natural language structure and natural language knowledge as its programming interface. The resulting architecture handles natural language environments using a combination of language models and natural language inference to bootstrap the agent’s reasoning. We empirically assess the efficiency gains of this combination while introducing a more intuitively programmed autonomous agent. Instructions in this interface substantially improve agent performance in the experimental scenario over a baseline agent created using a pure machine learning approach. The resulting architecture shows that combining learned policies with intuitively engineered domain knowledge yields substantial performance gains. We expect this class of agents to provide a powerful, yet intuitive, tool for agent-driven programming.

items.title: Navigating the Sea of Reviews: Unveiling the Effects of Introducing AI-Generated Summaries in E-Commerce
items.abstract: AI-generated review summaries are reshaping how consumers access product information, but their influence also extends to consumers who write reviews. Examining Amazon’s rollout of AI-generated review summaries, we find that these summaries encourage more review contributions and richer content. Consumers discuss product attributes absent from the summaries and elaborate on topics already covered. A controlled experiment suggests that summaries strengthen consumers’ belief that their contributions, together with others’, help future buyers make informed decisions. The increase in review contributions is stronger for products with many existing reviews or mixed ratings. Platform managers could prioritize summaries for products with mixed ratings, for which additional reviews can provide a more complete picture for future buyers. To build on richer review content, platforms could use writing prompts that highlight product attributes underrepresented in AI summaries. However, additional analyses suggest that AI summaries disproportionately benefit products that already sell well, potentially reinforcing sales concentration. Platforms could increase exposure for niche or new products, whereas policymakers could encourage fairness standards and periodic assessments of how AI-generated summaries affect product visibility and sales concentration. These findings highlight the potential of AI summaries to encourage consumer contributions, drawing attention to the risk of increased sales concentration.

items.title: Negative Belief Shifts After LLM-Written Arguments and the Limits of Lexical Cues: A Reanalysis of Two Public Benchmarks
items.abstract: Comparisons of human and LLM persuasion usually report average attitude change. We reanalyse the Anthropic persuasion dataset (3,939 ratings of 1,313 arguments on 56 policy claims, written by people or by five Claude models) at the level of arguments, because each argument was rated three times. On average, Claude 3 Opus arguments shifted support by 0.48 Likert points and human arguments by 0.54; the difference was not significant (p = 0.37), and equivalence held only for a ±0.20 margin. The distributions differed sharply. Of 1,120 Claude arguments, 221 moved at least one reader away from the advocated position, against 1 of 174 human arguments. The gap appeared in 54 of the 56 claims (Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel p = 6 × 10-10), with matched starting attitudes and similar rates across all five models. We then asked whether word-level cues often recommended for persuasive and search-visible writing (statistics, research terms, certainty, inclusive language) explain either outcome. They did not predict negative shifts, their associations with average change largely disappeared once prompt type and initial attitude were controlled, and neither word lists nor a full bag-of-words model predicted change on unseen claims (out-of-fold R2 ≤ 0.003). In GEO-bench (4,996 Google top-five pages for 1,000 queries), the same cues varied little with rank and mainly reflected query intent. Average persuasion scores can hide frequent opposite-direction responses to LLM text, and these responses are not visible in simple word counts.

items.title: Negotiating Control and Accountability among Stakeholders in High-Risk AI Use Cases: Development and Evaluation of the Method ALIGN
items.abstract: Characteristics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) severely restrict human control. This creates new challenges for socio-technical systems design especially in safety-critical domains, where control over risks is essential along with the accountability for any harm caused. Drawing from human factors and AI governance literature, expert interviews and participant observation in a complex high-risk AI use case from the railways, we developed ALIGN, a scenario-based method that supports the governance of and stakeholder involvement in AI development and implementation in three ways: raising awareness for potential accountability-control misalignments in socio-technical systems and their negative consequences, offering a structured approach to assessing the alignment between accountability and control for stakeholders in a given use case, and supporting effective design decisions to mitigate AI risks. We describe the iterative development and evaluation of ALIGN and discuss how this method promotes AI governance by highlighting the relevance of control-accountability alignment throughout the AI life cycle.

items.title: Nipple-Sparing Mastectomy in BRCA1/2 Carriers: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Breast Cancer Occurrence After Risk-Reducing and Therapeutic Procedures
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Nipple-sparing mastectomy (NSM) is increasingly performed in BRCA1/2 carriers, both for risk reduction and for treatment of breast cancer, but concern remains about glandular tissue left beneath the preserved nipple. We summarised the oncological outcomes of NSM in carriers. Methods: We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and Europe PubMed Central (Europe PMC) up to 30 September 2026, CENTRAL on 26 September 2026, and Embase on 7 November 2026 and screened the citations of relevant articles for series reporting outcomes of NSM in BRCA1/2 carriers. The outcomes were breast cancer diagnosed after risk-reducing NSM and locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM; cancers found at surgery were not counted. Proportions per woman were pooled with a binomial random-effects model (generalised linear mixed model, no continuity correction) and are reported as marginal (average-risk) and median-type (typical-study) proportions, with crude proportions, a beta-binomial model, follow-up strata, and approximate person-time analyses as checks. Two human reviewers went through all articles, with generative AI used only as an assistant, and the statistics were reviewed by a third author. Risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Joanna Briggs Institute checklist and certainty of evidence with GRADE. Results: Fifteen studies were included. After risk-reducing NSM, seven breast cancers occurred among 1215 women from eleven studies (crude proportion 0.58% (exact 95% CI 0.23–1.18%); model-based marginal proportion 0.60%, median-type 0.41% (95% CI 0.04–1.07%)); follow-up ranged from 33 to 129 months, and four of the seven cancers came from one international registry. After therapeutic NSM, locoregional recurrence occurred in 16 of 363 women from five studies (crude 4.4% (exact 95% CI 2.5–7.1%); model-based marginal proportion 4.3%, median-type 4.2% (95% CI 1.1–6.9%)); one study contributed 11 of the 16 events. Recurrence within the nipple–areolar complex was reported explicitly by only one study (none in 114 breasts). Sensitivity analyses yielded median-type proportions of 0.30% to 0.74% after risk-reducing NSM and 2.6% to 4.2% after therapeutic NSM. Risk of bias was moderate to high in most studies, and the certainty of the evidence was very low for both outcomes. Conclusions: In BRCA1/2 carriers, about 0.6% of women had breast cancer after risk-reducing NSM and about 4% had locoregional recurrence after therapeutic NSM, but follow-up was short and heterogeneous and the certainty of the evidence is very low. These data describe observed event frequencies and do not establish oncological safety or equivalence to other mastectomy techniques; longer prospective studies with time-to-event, gene-specific, and comparative reporting are needed.

items.title: O uso de Languaging nas aulas de Português como Língua de Herança
items.abstract: This study aims to discuss and analyze the use of Languaging as a tool for linguistic construction in the teaching and learning process of Portuguese as a Heritage Language. The Languaging process is examined through Language-Related Episodes (LREs), understood as analytical tools for investigating learners’ linguistic reflection and for supporting pedagogical practices in heritage language education, more specifically in Portuguese. The study is based on the analysis of interactions that occurred in a Portuguese as a Heritage Language classroom context with participants living in South Africa, aged between 10 and 11. The main findings indicate that the LREs identified in the study are predominantly related to grammatical aspects and structural mechanisms of writing, and they highlight the crucial role of teacher mediation in learners’ cognitive engagement. The conclusions suggest that the use of Languaging in collaborative writing activities constitutes a powerful analytical and pedagogical tool for Portuguese as a Heritage Language instruction, as it promotes the articulation between form, meaning, and discourse, fostering interculturality in the classroom, while also underscoring the need for teacher education specifically focused on heritage language instruction and sensitive to the linguistic and sociocultural particularities of heritage speakers.

items.title: Occupation-Specific Associations Between Psychosocial Stress and Low Back Pain Among Healthcare Workers: Evidence from Japan’s Mandatory Stress Check Program
items.abstract: Low back pain (LBP) is a common occupational health problem among healthcare workers. While physical demands are known to contribute to LBP, few large-scale studies have investigated the contribution of psychosocial stressors. This study examined the association between occupational LBP and stress-related factors at a university hospital in Japan. In this cross-sectional study, we analyzed responses to the Brief Job Stress Questionnaire administered to 2,450 staff members. Participants were categorized into LBP and non-LBP groups. The prevalence of LBP and high stress was compared by occupation. Multivariable logistic regression analysis was performed to identify factors independently associated with LBP. The overall prevalence of frequent LBP was 29.1%, being highest in nurses (39.3%) and lowest in doctors (11.1%). The odds ratio for LBP in nurses versus doctors was 3.54 (95% confidence interval 2.22–5.63). High stress status was more common in the LBP group than in the non-LBP group (25.1% versus 6.9%). Multivariate analysis showed that subjective physical workload, interpersonal stress in the workplace, physical fatigue, depressive symptoms, support from supervisors, work/life satisfaction, and body mass index were independently associated with LBP. These findings provide epidemiological evidence that both physical and psychosocial stressors are associated with occupational LBP among healthcare workers.

items.title: Occupational health and safety as a link between environmental safety and production efficiency: a moderated mediation analysis
items.abstract: Background Maintaining safe workplace environments in manufacturing industries is important for ensuring employees' health and maintaining effective production performance. Research on environmental safety and occupational health and safety is extensive, but the association between environmental safety and production efficiency and whether employees' safety knowledge supports this relationship, has received limited attention. Methods Data were collected from two independent cross-sectional purposive samples of footwear production workers (Wave 1 and Wave 2; N = 385 each), 3 months apart, and analyzed separately using Hayes PROCESS macro model 7 to investigate the indirect association between environmental safety and production efficiency through occupational health and safety, and the moderating effect of safety knowledge, with a simple slope test used to probe the interaction. Total effects were estimated using model 4. Results Contrary to the hypothesized direction, the association between environmental safety and occupational health and safety was weaker at higher safety knowledge in both waves; the interaction was significant after correction for multiple testing in Wave 1 only. In Wave 1, the interaction was a crossover: environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety only at low safety knowledge, and the indirect effect on production efficiency was significant only at low safety knowledge. The direct and total effects were not significant. In Wave 2, environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety at all levels of safety knowledge, with the association weakening as knowledge increased. The indirect effect was significant at low, mean and high safety knowledge, and the direct and total effects were also significant, indicating partial mediation. Conclusion In both waves, environmental safety was indirectly associated with production efficiency through occupational health and safety, at least among workers with lower safety knowledge, and this indirect association was weaker among workers with higher safety knowledge. These cross-sectional findings suggest that safe working environments may be particularly relevant for workers with lower safety knowledge.

items.title: Occupational Health and Safety Knowledge and Perceived Impact of Health Education Among Municipal Waste Workers in Calabar, Nigeria: An Exploratory Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Municipal solid waste workers operate in high-risk environments with limited institutional support, exposing them to diverse occupational hazards. This study explored occupational health and safety knowledge, practices, and experiences among municipal waste workers in Calabar, Nigeria, and examined the perceived impact of a health education intervention using a qualitative approach. A qualitative exploratory design was employed, involving Key Informant Interviews (KII) with 12 managers and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with 36 waste workers. Data were collected using semi-structured interview guides and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings revealed low baseline knowledge of occupational hazards, poor safety practices, and systemic barriers such as inadequate provision of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), weak monitoring, funding constraints, and poor prioritization of worker health. The intervention improved awareness and perceived understanding of occupational hazards and safety practices, although structural barriers persisted. The study concludes that health education enhances knowledge but must be complemented by systemic reforms, including provision of PPE, enforcement of safety policies, and improved worker welfare.

items.title: Occupational health and safety knowledge varies by settlement duration, residency status, and previous training among construction workers in Ontario, Canada
items.abstract: Introduction Occupational health and safety (OHS) knowledge is important for identifying worker training needs and informing workplace injury prevention strategies. However, immigrant workers are often treated as a homogeneous group despite differences in settlement duration, residency status, and previous training experiences that may influence their knowledge of workplace rights, responsibilities, and safe work practices. This exploratory study examined differences in OHS knowledge among immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years, immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years, and Canadian-born construction workers in Ontario, Canada. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 206 construction workers assessed OHS knowledge using scenario-based questions developed with reference to Ontario OHS requirements. Associations between OHS knowledge scores and participant characteristics were examined using univariable analyses and a generalized linear model. Results Immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years had higher OHS knowledge scores than immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years. Knowledge also differed by residency status, with Canadian citizens born outside Canada and permanent residents scoring higher than Canadian-born and temporary-resident participants. In the adjusted model, longer residence in Ontario, residency status, and previous OHS training outside Ontario were significantly associated with higher OHS knowledge scores. Discussion The findings demonstrate that OHS knowledge cannot be adequately characterized through a simple immigrant/non-immigrant distinction. Differences associated with settlement duration, residency status, and previous training highlight important heterogeneity among construction workers and may help identify OHS educational and prevention needs. Future research should evaluate whether targeted interventions addressing these differences improve safety practices and occupational health outcomes.

items.title: On Evaluating Performance of LLM Inference Systems
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.

items.title: Once Upon a Bias: Gender Stereotyping in LLM-Generated Children's Stories
items.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

items.title: One-Year Prediction of Vision-Threatening Diabetic Retinopathy Complications Using Multimodal Artificial Intelligence: A Multicenter Real-World Study
items.abstract: Current diabetic retinopathy management relies primarily on contemporaneous severity grading and does not directly quantify the short-term risk of vision-threatening complications. We developed and internally evaluated image-based artificial intelligence models for one-year prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity, proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and center-involved diabetic macular edema (ci-DME) using retinal imaging acquired during routine care.The prospective multicenter EviRed cohort included 3,183 patients with diabetes, 8,520 visits and 16,509 eye-level observations collected across 14 French hospitals. Device-specific ensembles were developed for ultra-widefield color fundus photography (CLARUS500 and OPTOS) and OCT angiography (CIRRUS5000 and PLEX Elite9000). Predictions from individual images and both eyes were aggregated at the patient-visit level. Participants were partitioned at the patient level into adevelopment set (65\%) and a held-out test set (35\%).For prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity at the subsequent annual visit, OPTOS and CLARUS500 achieved quadratic weighted kappa values of 0.866 (95\% confidence interval, 0.842--0.878) and 0.852 (0.830--0.877), respectively. For incident ci-DME, CIRRUS5000 achieved the highest discrimination (AUC, 0.826; 0.770--0.878), whereas PLEX Elite9000 yielded the highest AUC point estimate for incident PDR (0.877; 0.807--0.950). Late fusion did not consistently outperform the strongest device-specific model. In secondary complete-case analyses, observed ci-DME incidence increased across quartiles of the image-derived risk score, reaching 19.7--30.4\% in the highest-risk quartile. AI models also achieved higher AUC point estimates than unassisted expert risk assessments for both complications, although these comparisons were exploratory.Retinal imaging acquired at a single routine-care visit therefore contains information associated with diabetic retinopathy severity and vision-threatening complications one year later. These findings support image-based short-term risk stratification, while external validation, calibration and prospective clinical utility assessment remain necessary before deployment.

items.title: OpenConsult, an Open-Source Fully Local AI Scribe With Live Decision Support: Development and Formative Evaluation
items.abstract: Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.

items.title: OpenKAGE: Open-Ended Lifelong Learning in the Open World via Knowledge-Sharing Agent-Group Evolution
items.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

items.title: Opportunities and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence Use in Secondary School Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is entering the everyday work of secondary schools. Teachers encounter AI-based tools both in classroom organisation and in feedback or adaptation tasks. As these tools become more visible in school practice, their educational role and practical value need to be examined in relation to the conditions of real classrooms. This is especially relevant in classes with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in pace and readiness to participate. In these settings, AI may help teachers adapt instructional material and provide more individualised support. Its value, however, depends on professional judgement and on how each tool is connected to pedagogical purpose. This paper examines opportunities and challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. The planned study will use teachers’ accounts to examine how AI tools are understood and used in secondary school practice. It is designed as a qualitative inquiry based on semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers, with the interview material examined thematically. Through teachers’ accounts, the study will explore how AI is understood in relation to lesson preparation and student support, while also examining what makes its use difficult in day-to-day teaching. The paper approaches AI as a tool whose usefulness depends on classroom context and teachers’ pedagogical decisions.

items.title: OPPORTUNITIES FOR USING VIRTUAL AND AUGMENTED REALITY TECHNOLOGIES IN MILITARY AVIATION
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are moving from experimental demonstrations to operational tools in military aviation. This article examines the main opportunities these technologies offer in six areas: immersive flight and mission training, cockpit and helmet-mounted displays, live-virtual-constructive training, aircraft maintenance, mission planning and debriefing, and human-performance training. Using an analytical review of academic and professional literature, the study compares the potential benefits of each application area with its principal technical and human-factors limitations. The findings show that VR offers the clearest near-term value in cost-effective procedural and tactical training, while AR offers the greatest long-term value in airborne information display and in maintenance support. Simulator sickness, latency, registration accuracy, cybersecurity and the need for validated transfer-of-training evidence remain the key barriers. The article concludes with practical recommendations for armed forces and military education institutions that wish to adopt these technologies in a phased and evidence-based way.

items.title: Participation without power: urban biodiversity plans exclude the communities most affected by biodiversity loss
items.abstract: Urban biodiversity loss is increasingly framed as a governance challenge with intertwined ecological and social dimensions, yet little is known about who participates in local biodiversity planning, what authority that participation carries, and whether plans recognize and address disproportionate harms. This study presents the first comparative analysis at this scale of participation in Local Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (LBSAPs), examining 98 plans from 98 municipalities across 26 countries. Using a hybrid methodology combining large language model-assisted verbatim extraction with manual coding (96.4% extraction accuracy), plans were assessed across four dimensions: participant recognition, participatory mechanisms, authorship, and transparency. Of the 98 plans, 71 (72%) documented some participatory mechanism, but only 18 (18%) granted participants any authority over plan content, and only 2 (2%) shared control over resources. Authorship was concentrated in city governments (93 of 98 plans), and 39 cities (40%) provided no transparency about participatory processes. Knowledge-holder positioning was dominated by scientists (M = 0.60 on a 0–1 scale) while Indigenous peoples (M = 0.08), marginalized groups (M = 0.01), and youth (M = 0.03) were systematically excluded. A distributive analysis revealed a marginalized-specific redress gap: 16 plans recognized marginalized groups as bearing environmental harm, but only 4 of those plans offered programmatic response; a 75% recognition-without-remedy rate not seen for any other actor type. These findings indicate that prevailing LBSAP governance architectures may constrain conservation effectiveness, by excluding the situated knowledge of communities most affected by biodiversity loss, and may reproduce environmental injustice, by acknowledging disproportionate harms without acting on them. Governance reforms that meaningfully redistribute participatory authority are needed to advance both biodiversity outcomes and equitable urban conservation.

items.title: Patent Application: HYBRID CLASSICAL-QUANTUM PROCESS FOR THE IN SILICO RECOMBINATION OF PLANT GENOMES WITH EVALUATION BY MEANS OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
items.abstract: Plant genomics with a hybrid classical-quantum model Artificial intelligence and quantum computing for the digital design of plant genomes Italian patent application no. 102026000034324, filed on 18 November 2026. Inventor, applicant and sole rights holder: Paolo Ciccolella. This invention proposes combining artificial intelligence and quantum computing to explore possible combinations of plant DNA and identify those worth investigating further. For businesses interested in plant genomics, the idea is to provide early guidance for computational design: turning a vast number of possibilities into selected, evaluated and documented digital candidates. The challenge is easy to picture. If DNA is a large instruction book, studying alternative versions of some passages means comparing many combinations. Three alternatives for each of twenty regions already produce more than three billion possibilities. The method tackles this complexity by dividing the work between a classical computer, two AI models and a quantum search component. HOW THE HYBRID MODEL WORKS The idea is to choose one alternative for each DNA region being studied, put the choices together and evaluate the resulting combination. Everything happens on a computer. The process follows six steps. • Prepare the data. The computer starts with a digital version of the plant’s DNA, called a reference genome. It identifies the regions to study and organises the available alternative sequences for each one, recording where they come from. • Give each alternative an initial score. The first AI model examines each alternative separately. Having learned from other cases, it can provide guidance before any complete combination in the new case has been evaluated. The computer also measures similarity between the ends of sequences that will be placed next to one another. These scores and measurements define the selection problem. [B12] • Search for combinations. The quantum component receives this problem expressed in numbers. It uses QAOA, an algorithm whose role is to propose combinations while seeking to favour those with better scores. Qubits represent the possible choices; the DNA sequences remain on the classical computer, which sets and updates the algorithm’s parameters. [B11] • Evaluate the whole combination. The computer checks that each combination selects exactly one alternative per region and assembles valid choices into a digital candidate. The second AI model evaluates the complete candidate, including relationships between its parts that the first AI model could not observe when examining them separately. • Guide the next search. The system compares the overall evaluation with the score predicted at the start and uses the difference to update the search. When only a few results are available, it limits the correction’s influence to avoid relying too heavily on sparse information. • Return verifiable proposals. For each selected candidate, the system retains the chosen sequences, their provenance and the evaluations performed. It also records a digital fingerprint, a code used to check the content. Researchers can reconstruct the proposal and understand how it was selected. If necessary data are missing, the system flags this. A concrete example: the patent uses the digital reference for Micro-Tom tomato and considers three regions, each with three alternatives created for the test. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible combinations. The search uses a nine-qubit quantum circuit simulated on a classical computer. This tests the computational method without producing plants. [B14] INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS The patent describes the production of verifiable digital representations of candidate genomes. Its industrial role lies in designing and selecting hypotheses, ahead of experimental work. Applications across sectors require data and models suited to the objectives under study. • NGT and assisted evolution techniques. NGTs, or new genomic techniques, include approaches known in Italy as TEA, meaning assisted evolution techniques, which enable targeted changes to genetic material. The proposed method could support research by comparing genomic hypotheses before experimental work. For seed and biotechnology companies, the prospect is to build a reasoned set of digital candidates for further investigation within NGT/TEA programmes. • Seed industry and variety development. For seed companies and research teams, the method could support the preliminary selection of combinations for further study. Research objectives could include drought or salinity tolerance, disease resistance and yield stability. Its contribution would be to establish research priorities while preserving the reasoning behind them. • Fresh produce and food processing. Computational design could focus on commercial characteristics such as product quality, shelf life and processing suitability. Tomato, pepper and aubergine are examples of supply chains that future projects could address, connecting growers’ and processors’ needs with the criteria used to evaluate candidates. • Nutraceuticals and plant ingredients. One possible development concerns plants of interest for functional ingredients, extracts and bioactive compounds. The method could explore genomic combinations in programmes focused, for example, on pigments or plant metabolites, providing documented candidates to guide subsequent analysis. • Plant biotechnology and industrial raw materials. For crops intended for oils, fibres or biomass, the method could help compare genomic hypotheses against supply chain objectives. Reconstructible digital records would support information exchange between teams developing the models and those planning subsequent experimental work. • Bioinformatics and computing centres. The most direct application is within the information systems of laboratories, computing centres and plant genomics businesses. The process could underpin software modules or analytical services that explore combinations and return candidates with scores and execution logs, integrating quantum search into the workflow. items.title: Patient perceptions of artificial intelligence in MRI reconstruction: A mixed methods study from a single NHS trust
items.abstract: Introduction As part of a strategy to increase magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) capacity, the UK government funded the purchase of manufacturer artificial intelligence (AI) MRI image reconstruction software on MRI scanners. It aimed to reduce scan duration without compromising image quality and has been widely installed on clinical MRI scanners across the UK. Methods This is a mixed methods study, using an initial questionnaire to quantify opinions followed by focus groups of responders to further explore their views on technical issues. Patient views on the use of AI in MRI image reconstruction for reducing acquisition times, and more generally in their MRI pathway, were assessed. Results Study participants prefer improved image quality over faster acquisition times. If reducing acquisition times with AI, they feel it should only be used if extremely accurate images can be ascertained. They are uncomfortable with the use of manufacturer AI software for image reconstruction where accuracy is not stated and would like to be told about the use of AI in MRI. Conclusions Many participants felt that manufacturer AI software for MRI image reconstruction may be used only if a high accuracy is demonstrated, and if the training data is representative of the patient population, to not exacerbate health inequalities. This information is not currently given by manufacturers, which made the patient representatives concerned. Implication for practice •Local validation of AI image reconstruction software may make patients more confident about its use. •AI patient information materials should be accessible and discuss accuracy, and radiographers can be trained to help inform and reassure patients. •Engagement with all clinical stakeholders in MRI should be undertaken to understand their views on AI, and how manufacturer AI software should be implemented.

items.abstract: Over the past decade, the innovative convergence of cloud computing, natural language processing (NLP), and large language models (LLM) has triggered a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction. This study aims to conceptually review and propose a research design to objectively analyze the effect of security and privacy perceptions on the use of AI as a venting medium. The proposed method is a conceptual quantitative research design with a correlational approach, planned for Generation Z respondents. Based on a literature synthesis of referenced studies, the findings indicate a highly significant positive correlation between dispositional shame and self-disclosure to artificial intelligence (r = 0.337, p < 0.001, n = 182). The conceptual review concludes that AI operates effectively as a complementary screening instrument but risks triggering an atrophy of social resilience, thus necessitating juridical protection through the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP).

items.title: Perceived Benefits and Reported Uses of Generative AI for Accessibility: An Exploratory Survey of Minnesota Educators
items.abstract: Digital inclusion with generative AI depends not only on educators’ access to tools but on how they use them. Comparing the benefits educators perceive with the uses they report may reveal gaps between what educators believe AI can do and how they use it in teaching. In this exploratory secondary analysis of survey data from 293 Minnesota PK-12 and higher education educators, we compared endorsement of improved accessibility for diverse learners as a benefit of generative AI with reported use of AI to enhance accessibility for students with disabilities. Because the items differ in scope and target population, the comparison describes response proportions, not a failure to act on a belief. Among 160 AI-using educators who answered both items, 133 (83.1%) endorsed the benefit and 51 (31.9%) reported the use (McNemar exact p < 0.001). Subgroup differences were not detected, though power was limited. Among all AI users, self-rated competence was associated with reported accessibility use (44.0% vs. 27.9%; adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI [1.13, 4.73]); among endorsers, the estimate was imprecise. Keyword-selected open-ended responses more often described general differentiation and language support than disability-specific use. We discuss measurement implications and propose supports as hypotheses for evaluation.

items.title: Perceived impact of generative artificial intelligence on clinical learning and decision-making among internal medicine residents in Ethiopia: a mixed- methods study
items.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.
